question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't settle whether you must be present, and they say nothing about a $90 rebooking fee. They do set limits on when the provider can enter and what the smoke alarm duties are.

I applied the law in force on 3 December 2025: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* Authorised Version No. 111 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* Authorised Version No. 005 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Both were in force from 25 November 2025. I didn't rely on the later versions in the results.

### What the law says

- **Smoke alarm duty:** The provider must ensure any smoke alarm is "correctly installed and in working condition," has batteries, and is "tested at least once every 12 months in accordance with any instructions by the manufacturer of the smoke alarm" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The provider or agent must "immediately arrange for the repairs to be carried out" if an alarm doesn't meet these requirements [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Entry for this purpose:** The provider may enter "to do an inspection but not more than once every 12 months" and "to comply with the rental provider's duties under the Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm test falls under those duties [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Duty to allow entry:** "The renter must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Do you have to be there?

The retrieved documents don't say whether a renter must be personally present. The Act's entry provisions (the notice and manner-of-entry rules) aren't in the in-force excerpts I retrieved, so I can't confirm the rule. Your obligation is to allow entry where proper procedure has been followed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Can they charge $90?

No retrieved document mentions a rebooking fee for inspections, so I can't say it's lawful or unlawful. The smoke alarm duty is placed on the provider [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and nothing I found shifts the cost of the check to the renter.

### What you can do or ask

- **Check the 12-month limit.** If an entry for an inspection has already happened in the past 12 months, the provider's right to inspect for that purpose may not apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Note that one excerpt labelled Authorised Version 005 gives a 6-month limit for the same provision, so check the authorised text before relying on either figure.
- **Ask for the basis in writing.** Ask the agent which duty requires entry, what the fee is based on, and where it is authorised.
- **Offer other times.** The provider may enter "at any time, if the renter has agreed within the last 7 days" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can agree to a different time, but the documents don't say the provider must accept a set window.
- **Get help.** The Regulations list Consumer Affairs Victoria on 1300 55 81 81 for contract questions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- Whether you must be personally present.
- The notice period and delivery rules for entry under the in-force Act.
- Whether a rebooking fee can be charged for a smoke alarm check.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 15 January 2026, the app most likely cannot charge you a card fee for paying rent. The documents don't expressly say that a card surcharge is covered, so that conclusion is my reading of the wording. Who receives the fee doesn't change the answer, because the prohibition applies to any person who demands or receives the charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Version applied:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, version 111 (file rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf), in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations version in force is *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, version 005, in force until 9 February 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Card fees (s 51(3)(b)):** A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge or indemnity for a charge relating to "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This is the provision most relevant to a card surcharge, though the documents don't say whether a card fee counts as a charge for "use" of an electronic payment facility.
- **Fee-free method (s 42(4)):** The provider or agent must ensure that a payment method incurring no additional costs (other than the renter's bank or account fees) is reasonably available. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A manual bank transfer with no fee fits this description, as you describe it. The documents say nothing about speed, so slowness isn't a legal reason to refuse it.
- **Cost disclosure (s 42(7)):** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Electronic transfer (s 42(5) and reg 19):** Providers must permit Centrepay and any prescribed payment method. Regulation 19 prescribes electronic funds transfer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't clearly say whether a manual bank transfer is an electronic funds transfer, so you should not rely on this point alone.
- **Application and rent payment fees (s 51A):** The version 111 text prohibits fees for prescribed matters, including rent payment "other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the list of prescribed matters is in regulation 21C, which "has effect on and after 31 March 2026" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). So this prohibition does not appear to apply yet on 15 January 2026.

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

Not under s 51(3)(b), which applies to anyone who demands or receives the charge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Under s 42(4), the duty to provide a no-cost method falls on the provider or agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address whether an app company that is not the agent is bound by s 42. The s 51A rule that would reach a business such as an app company does not yet apply, as noted above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the agent in writing what each payment method costs, since they must tell you before you consent to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. Confirm in writing that the fee-free bank transfer is available, since s 42(4) requires it to be reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. You are not required to accept a fee-bearing card method as the only option. The documents don't say you must consent to any particular method.
4. If you pay by bank transfer and want a receipt, you can request one at the time of payment. For a payment not made in person, the receipt must be given within 5 business days of receiving the payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

The documents don't say what remedies apply if the app charges a fee anyway, or which body to complain to. I can't answer that from these sources.

**Later versions (not applied)**

The documents include *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* version 009 (in force from 30 June 2026) [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf) and *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* version 115 (in force from 13 October 2026) [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf). Neither was in force on 15 January 2026, so I haven't relied on them.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both required points are present. The answer says a no-cost payment method must be reasonably available under s 42(4) and that a manual bank transfer with no fee 'fits this description'. For the hardest point, it says the list of prescribed matters in reg 21C 'has effect on and after 31 March 2026', so 'this prohibition does not appear to apply yet on 15 January 2026'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. Neither failure condition is asserted: on s 51A the answer says reg 21C "has effect on and after 31 March 2026" and so "this prohibition does not appear to apply yet on 15 January 2026", resting its card-fee conclusion on s 51(3)(b) instead, and on the fee-free method it affirms that "a payment method incurring no additional costs... is reasonably available" under s 42(4).

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 111' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 005' (with links 97-109aa111 and 21-3sra005), and applies rules only from those in-force versions; it mentions version 009 and version 115 only to say they were not in force and not relied on.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found show that the damp and mould may count as urgent repairs under the Act. They do not cover cancelling the lease or getting a rent reduction for these defects.

**Which law applies:** On 15 October 2019, the version in force is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The regulation versions I retrieved all started in 2022 or later, so none of them is the law on your date [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[7]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-06/21-3sra009-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)[[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says:**
- One of the Act's objectives is to provide "safe and habitable premises to renters" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The amending text in Version 088 replaces the urgent repairs definition so that it includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure", including "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure". It also adds "a failure to comply with any rental minimum standards" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpt shows this as amending text, so I can't confirm the full consolidated wording.
- "Rental minimum standards" are "the standards prescribed under section 65A" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't include those 2019 standards, so I can't say whether damp, mould or rotting timber breaches them.
- A lease term that tries to exclude or restrict the Act, or the exercise of a right under it, is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**Your options:**

1. **Ask for repairs:** Damp or mould caused by the building structure may be an urgent repair under the definition above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents mention a 7-day "required time" for certain duties under sections 60 and 67 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). However, the excerpts don't contain the text of those sections, so I can't confirm that this deadline covers your situation. The documents also don't set out the notice steps or the VCAT application process for 2019.
2. **Cancel the lease:** The documents don't address termination rights for defects found before you move in, so I can't say whether you can cancel.
3. **Ask for lower rent:** The documents don't provide a rent reduction remedy for defects. The only rent-reduction reference is a prohibited term: a lease term that reduces rent when the renter has not breached the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That provision doesn't address your situation.

**Gaps and next steps:**
- The transitional rules in Schedule 1 say that some 2018 amendments don't apply to agreements entered into before the relevant amendment commenced [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't state when those amendments commenced, so check whether they apply to your lease.
- Get advice from the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) or Consumer Affairs Victoria. These sources are not in the documents I retrieved.

It also does not state the landlord's s 68 duty to keep the premises in good repair. It never says that cancellation turns on disrepair or unfitness rather than mere uncleanliness, or that photos or an inspection are the evidence.

It hedges that damp or mould 'may be an urgent repair', notes the provision is only 'amending text' whose consolidated wording it 'can't confirm', and says it 'can't say whether damp, mould or rotting timber breaches' the standards.

The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019', and every rule it applies is cited to that version [1]; the 2022-or-later regulation versions appear only to say they were not in force on 15 October 2019.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't include the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* version in force on 8 November 2022. The closest match I found is the Regulations, which I can answer from. Before you pay, check the points below.

**What the law says (Regulations, in force on 8 November 2022)**

The *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version **002** (in force from 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024), is the version that covers your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Its standard lease form says:

- The rental provider's details and their agent's details must be recorded, and "The rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if any of this information changes" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- The rental provider ticks the payment methods they accept. They "must permit a fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method and must allow the renter to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- "The renter is entitled to receive a receipt from the rental provider confirming payment of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- For bonds, the rental provider or their agent "must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA)" within 10 business days of receiving payment. If you don't receive an RTBA receipt within 15 business days of paying, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 13 71 64 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What to check before paying the new account**

1. **Get written notice of the change.** Ask the agent or owner to confirm in writing that the owner is now managing the property and is your rental provider. Under the form, a change in provider or agent details must be notified to you within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Check the payment method is fee-free.** The rental provider must offer at least one fee-free method (other than your own bank fees), and must allow Centrepay or another electronic transfer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Ask whether the new account incurs any fees.
3. **Verify the bank details independently.** Confirm the account name and BSB/account number by calling the owner on a number you already have, not one in the email. This is general good practice and is not stated in the documents.
4. **Confirm the bond is lodged.** Your bond was paid through the agent, so check that it was lodged with the RTBA. If you don't have an RTBA receipt, contact the RTBA using the details above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Keep receipts.** Ask for a receipt for each rent payment, as you are entitled to one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**Limits of what I can confirm**

- The Act's rules on changing payment methods and on disclosing payment costs appear in the 2019 text of the Act [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), but that version was not in force on 8 November 2022, so I can't confirm those rules applied on your date. The other Act versions retrieved (2019–2020, 2025 and 2026) are also outside that date [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)[[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/d98b58cd-fe91-3f90-92dd-3ce1ff4a6eb0_97-109aa089%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)[[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).
- The documents don't say what happens to your lease, your rights or the bond when a property moves from an agent to an owner-managed arrangement. You should check that with Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advisor, and get the 2022 version of the Act to confirm the position.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say whether you must be home in person, and they don't mention a $90 rebooking fee. I can't confirm either point from them.

Applying the law as at 3 December 2025, the relevant documents are the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 111, in force from 25 November 2025) [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 005, in force from 25 November 2025) [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I didn't use later versions.

### What the law says

- **Smoke alarms are the provider's job.** The provider must ensure any smoke alarm is correctly installed and working, has batteries, and is tested at least once every 12 months per the manufacturer's instructions [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Mains-powered testing must be done by a suitably qualified person [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Entry rules in the Regulations.** The rental provider may enter to do an inspection, but not more than once every 12 months, and at any time if the renter has agreed within the last 7 days [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The renter must allow entry where the provider has followed proper procedure [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Do you have to be there yourself?

The documents don't say. The Regulations only say you must allow entry when the provider has followed proper procedure [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The notice and timing rules in the current version of the Act (sections 85–88) aren't in the excerpts I retrieved, so I can't tell you what that procedure requires, including whether a 10 am–12:30 pm window is valid or whether you must attend.

### Can they charge the $90?

Nothing in the retrieved text authorises a rebooking fee for a smoke alarm check. The only fee-related provision I found concerns consent to assignment or sub-letting, which doesn't apply here [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I can't say the fee is unlawful, only that the documents don't support it.

### What you can do

- **Ask the agent for the legal basis in writing**, including the notice and the proper procedure they say they followed.
- **Agree a time.** Entry at a time you've agreed within the last 7 days is permitted [[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so offering a specific weekday time may resolve the issue.
- **Raise any smoke alarm fault.** If an alarm doesn't meet the requirements, you can request urgent repairs, and the provider or agent must immediately arrange them [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[8]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. Under the version of the Act in force on 15 January 2026, a landlord or agent must keep a no-extra-cost payment method reasonably available, and the law generally bars charging a fee for paying rent electronically. Whether a fee charged by a third-party app is covered is less clear from the text.

**Which law applies:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111 (in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026), is the version for your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A later Version 115 is dated from 13 October 2026, so it does not apply to you [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**

- **Fee-free method must be available.** The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method that "incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your manual bank transfer appears to meet this. The text says nothing about speed, so being slower does not by itself make it unavailable.
- **No charge for electronic payment facilities.** A person "must not demand or receive from a renter a charge or indemnity for a charge in relation to... the use of... any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This wording does not limit the charge to the landlord or agent.
- **Fees by businesses.** A business other than a provider, an agent, or an authorised deposit-taking institution must not "demand or receive a fee for any prescribed matter" in relation to paying rent. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The app company is not one of the exempt categories [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the retrieved text does not list which matters are "prescribed," so I cannot confirm that a card fee is one of them.
- **Disclosure.** Before you agree to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, including "third party transaction fees" and "any other electronic payment facility fees" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who receives the fee?**

The documents suggest it may matter, but they do not settle it:

- The s 51A exemption covers the provider and agent, so an agent's fee falls outside that section [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The s 51(3)(b) ban on electronic payment charges, however, applies to "a person" generally [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Section 42(7) refers to third-party transaction fees as costs the renter "may incur," which suggests the Act expects some third-party costs to exist and must be disclosed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Whether an app's fee is a banned charge or only a disclosable one is not answered by the retrieved text.

**What you can do**

1. Ask the agent in writing for the exact fee and who receives it, as s 42(7) requires disclosure before you consent to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. Ask them to confirm that the bank transfer option is available and fee-free, as s 42(4) requires [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations' standard form also says the provider "must permit a fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
3. If they refuse, you can raise it with Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT. The retrieved documents do not describe those steps in detail, so check them directly.
4. Ask for a written receipt. If you request one when paying, it must be given within 5 business days, and the penalty for not providing it is 25 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Limits of this answer:** The documents do not say whether a particular app's card fee is a "prescribed matter" or a banned "electronic payment facility" charge. A tenancy adviser or VCAT would need to decide that for your specific fee.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents do not contain enough to answer whether you can cancel, or whether you can get a rent reduction, for conditions found before you move in. They do show that damp, mould and structural faults can count as urgent repairs, and that the Act's protections cannot be contracted out of.

**Version applied:** On 15 October 2019, the version in force is the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 088), which applied from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The later versions (No. 101 from 2022 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) and No. 111 from 2025 [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf) were not in force on that date, so I have not relied on them.

**What the law says**

- The Act's objectives include "safe and habitable premises" for renters [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- "Urgent repairs" includes "any fault or damage that makes rented premises... unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The 2019 text of that definition, as shown in the retrieved excerpt, does not expressly list mould or damp. Text that does list "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" appears in the amendment provisions in the same document [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), and the later version lists it expressly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I could not confirm from the excerpt when that amendment took effect, so you should check this before relying on it.
- A term in a lease that purports to exclude or restrict the Act's provisions, or the exercise of a right under the Act, is invalid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- For urgent repairs, the "required time" for a duty under section 60 or 67 is 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpt does not say what sections 60 or 67 require.

**Your options, as far as the documents show**

- **Repairs:** The documents support treating serious damp or structural faults as a matter for the landlord to repair, and the 7-day "required time" applies to the section 60 and 67 duties [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The excerpt does not set out the step-by-step repair request process, and I cannot confirm that the timeframe applies to your specific defects.
- **Lower rent:** The Act says a lease must not include a term reducing rent if the renter does not breach the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That concerns lease terms, not a tribunal's power to reduce rent for defects. The documents do not say whether you can seek a rent reduction for these conditions, so I cannot answer this part.
- **Cancelling:** The documents do not include a provision allowing you to end a lease because of conditions found before move-in. I cannot answer this part from them.

**What I could not find:** the 2019 minimum standards for mould and dampness (the 2021 Regulations contain one, but they were not in force on 15 October 2019 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-07/21-3sra004-authorised.pdf)); the procedure for issuing a repair request; and any early-termination or rent-reduction remedy. The Tribunal, which is the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), is the body that resolves disputes under the Act, but the documents do not describe the process for bringing a claim. A lawyer or the Tribunal should confirm the remedies available to you before you act.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Before paying the new account, confirm in writing that the owner is your landlord and that the account is theirs, and confirm your bond is held with the RTBA. The 2022 documents I can access don't cover the rent-payment rules in full, so I can't confirm everything about the new payment arrangement.

**Which law applies on 8 November 2022**

- The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 101 (in force 7 September 2022 to 23 May 2023), applies [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 002 (in force 1 June 2022 to 30 November 2024), applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What the law says about the change**

- The standard lease form says the rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the provider's or agent's details change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- The form also says the rental provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees), and must allow payment through Centrepay or another electronic funds transfer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- The renter is entitled to a receipt confirming rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- The lease form says the agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days after receiving it, and the RTBA sends the renter a bond receipt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What to check before paying the new account**

1. **Get written notice from the owner.** Ask for a written notice that identifies the owner as the rental provider and gives their contact details. The lease form requires notice of changes within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Verify the bank details independently.** Confirm the account name matches the owner's name and call the owner or agent on a phone number you already have, not one from the new email. This is general good practice, not something the documents require.
3. **Check the payment method.** It should be fee-free apart from your own bank fees. Ask what fees apply before you pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If it isn't, ask for an alternative such as Centrepay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask for a receipt for each payment.** You're entitled to one [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Confirm your bond.** Check that the bond was lodged with the RTBA. If you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days of paying it, you can email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A change of manager doesn't change where your bond is held.

**What the documents don't cover**

- The 2022 Act (Version 101) excerpt I retrieved covers only ss 91ZN–91ZO on failure to pay bond. It doesn't include the Act's rent-payment (s 42) or bond (Part 10) provisions as they stood in November 2022. Later versions contain those sections, but they aren't the law for your date, so I haven't relied on them.
- The documents don't say whether a change of landlord requires a new lease or a variation of your existing one.

If the owner's new arrangement raises a dispute, you may want to contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advice service, since this answer is based only on the retrieved excerpts.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?

**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say you must be home in person. They also don't mention any $90 rebooking fee, so I can't confirm you can be charged it. I've applied the versions in force on 3 December 2025: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* Authorised Version No. 111 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* version 005 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

Smoke alarms must be correctly installed, working, fitted with batteries, and tested at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Mains-powered smoke alarms must be tested by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

It also says entry at a time agreed with the renter is allowed if the renter consented within 7 days before entry [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?

- **Repairs:** A renter's request for urgent repairs is possible for premises that don't meet the rental minimum standards on or immediately after moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf). The landlord's duty to keep premises in good repair applies "whether or not the renter was aware of any disrepair … before entering into occupation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

- **Non-urgent repairs:** The renter may apply to VCAT if repairs are not done "within 14 days of receiving notice" [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The documents I retrieved do not contain a general right to a rent reduction for disrepair.
- **Cancelling:** The retrieved documents do not contain a right to cancel a lease because of damp, mould or rotting timber. question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents I found don't say how a rent payment account change must be handled. They do set out duties on the rental provider and the bond that you can check before paying. These come from the versions in force on 8 November 2022: the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Version 101) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Version 002) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). I haven't used the later Act version (Version 110), which took effect in August 2025 [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Change of agent or contact details:** The standard lease forms say the rental provider "must notify the renter within 7 days if any of this information changes," and that information includes the rental provider's details and the agent's details [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the owner takes over management, this notice requirement applies.
- **Payment methods:** The forms say the rental provider "must permit a fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method and must allow the renter to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer." The renter is also "entitled to receive a receipt from the rental provider confirming payment of rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Your bond:** A rental provider who receives a bond must hold it on trust for the renter until it is paid to the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The provider must give the bond to the RTBA within 10 business days after receiving it, together with the completed bond lodgment form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The RTBA must then send a receipt within 7 days [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, you may notify the RTBA [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

### What to check before paying the new account

1. **Written notice of the change:** Ask for written confirmation that the owner is now managing the property and that the agent is no longer acting for them. Under the forms, the provider must notify you of changed details within 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Identity of the new account holder:** Confirm the account is in the owner's name (the rental provider named in your agreement). The documents don't address this, so it is general advice, not a legal requirement from these sources.
3. **Fee-free payment option:** Check that the owner offers a fee-free method other than cash, or Centrepay/electronic transfer, as the forms require [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Receipts:** Make sure you will receive a receipt for each rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Your bond:** Confirm the bond was lodged with the RTBA and that you received the bond lodgment form and the RTBA receipt [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you don't have the RTBA receipt, the documents say you may contact the RTBA (email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 per the form) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

### What the documents don't cover

- How to verify that bank details are genuine, or what to do if they look suspicious.
- Whether you can withhold rent or change how you pay if the owner doesn't give notice.
- Any rule about a change of owner ending the agency arrangement, or about the bond being transferred when management changes. The retrieved excerpts don't address this.

If you're unsure, contact Consumer Affairs Victoria or the RTBA. The retrieved documents don't name Consumer Affairs as a dispute body, so I can't confirm their role from these sources.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
## What the law says

On **3 December 2025**, the applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111, in force 25 November 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 005, in force 25 November 2025** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must ensure that smoke alarms are correctly installed, working, fitted with batteries, and tested at least every 12 months. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The prescribed rental-agreement summary also says the rental provider may enter to comply with duties under the Act, and that the renter must allow entry when the proper procedure has been followed. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved documents **do not say that the renter personally must be present** to let an inspector in. They also **do not contain any authority for, or rule about, charging a $90 rebooking fee**. The documents likewise do not specify that a smoke-alarm appointment must be on a weekday between 10:00 am and 12:30 pm. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

You can ask the agent:

1. **What legal provision requires you personally to be present**, rather than allowing entry by an agreed method or another authorised person; and  
2. **What legal or contractual basis authorises the $90 fee**, including an itemised explanation of the alleged cost.

Based on the retrieved documents alone, you cannot be told that you must personally attend or that the agent can charge the $90.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says — 15 January 2026

On that date, the applicable Act was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111, in force from 25 November 2025**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The applicable regulations were the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider or agent **must ensure that a rent-payment method with no additional cost**—apart from bank or account fees on your own bank account—is **reasonably available** to you. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) Therefore, the app may charge a card-payment fee **only if** the no-fee bank-transfer option is reasonably available. The fact that the transfer is slower is not addressed in the retrieved documents, so they do not say whether that makes it unreasonable.

Before you consent to use a payment method, the rental provider or agent must tell you about costs you may incur, including **third-party transaction fees** and **other electronic payment facility fees**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The documents do not say that the result changes depending on whether the fee is retained by the app company or paid to the agent. They also do not expressly state who is legally entitled to receive such a fee.

The prescribed rental agreement form confirms that at least one payment method must be fee-free, apart from the renter’s own bank fees, and refers to bank deposit or another electronic funds transfer as available payment options. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- Ask the agent or rental provider to confirm in writing that the bank-transfer option is the required **fee-free payment method** and that it is reasonably available. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Ask for the card fee and any other payment-method costs to be disclosed in writing before using the card option. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- Ask whether the fee is a third-party transaction fee or electronic payment facility fee, and who receives it. The documents require cost information but do not provide a rule answering the recipient question. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- If the transfer option is not reasonably available in practice, the retrieved documents do not provide a specific procedure or test for resolving that issue.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## Law on 15 October 2019

The applicable document is **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 088**—in force from **2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The Act required the landlord to keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit and suitable for occupation. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) The documents also identify **mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure** as an urgent repair where it makes the premises unsafe or insecure. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

However, the retrieved Authorised Version 088 does **not** contain the specific provision dealing with a renter terminating before taking possession because premises are not in good repair or fit for habitation. A later version contains such a provision, but it was not the version in force on 15 October 2019, so I cannot confirm from these documents that you could cancel under that provision in 2019. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for repairs:** Give the landlord or agent written notice immediately, describing the damp, mould and rotting timber and attaching photographs or other evidence. The retrieved documents support the landlord’s repair obligation, but they do not provide the full Authorised Version 088 procedure or time limits for pursuing ordinary repairs. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

- **Treat the mould or damp as urgent if it is structural and makes the property unsafe or insecure:** The 2019 document identifies this as an urgent-repair category. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not contain enough of the Authorised Version 088 text to confirm the precise process, spending limit or reimbursement amount applicable on 15 October 2019.

- **Ask for lower rent:** You can ask the landlord to agree to a rent reduction, but the retrieved Authorised Version 088 documents do **not** establish a right to a reduced rent merely because the premises have these defects. They do show a mechanism for applying to have rent paid into a **Rent Special Account** where repairs have not been carried out, but the retrieved text is from later versions and cannot be treated as the law in force on your date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2021-03/97-109aa098%20authorised.pdf)

- **Cancel the lease:** The retrieved Authorised Version 088 documents do not contain enough information to confirm that you could unilaterally cancel before moving in. Do not simply stop paying or abandon the agreement without obtaining written agreement from the landlord or a decision from the relevant tribunal. The documents do not state the legal consequence of handing back the keys in this situation.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

On **8 November 2022**, the retrieved document in force was **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002 (in force from 1 June 2022)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Your residential rental agreement should state:

- the rental provider’s name and contact details;
- the agent’s name and contact details, if an agent is acting; and
- the permitted rent-payment methods and payment details. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The form says the rental provider must notify you **within 7 days if any of that information changes**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) It also says the rental provider must allow at least one **fee-free payment method** (apart from your own bank fees) and must allow electronic funds transfer or Centrepay. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** specifically say that an owner may, or may not, take over rent collection from an agency during an existing lease. They also do not prescribe a bank-account verification procedure. The retrieved Residential Tenancies Act document is **Authorised Version 110**, in force only from **6 August 2025**, so it cannot establish the law applying on your stated date. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-08/97-109aa110-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask before paying

Before transferring rent, ask the agent and owner to provide written confirmation of:

1. **Who is now managing the tenancy**, including the owner’s full name and contact details and confirmation that the agency’s authority to collect rent has ended. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
2. **The new payment details**, and whether they are a change to the payment details in your signed agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
3. **The effective date** from which payments should go to the new account.
4. **A receipt or written record for your first payment**, and confirmation that the bond has been lodged with the RTBA.

Do not treat the new bank details alone as proof of the change. Independently contact the agency using the contact details in your signed lease or previous correspondence, and contact the owner through independently verified details before paying. The documents do not state this as a specific legal requirement; it is a prudent precaution because they do not provide a bank-account verification process.

For the bond you already paid, check that it was lodged with the RTBA within **10 business days**. The RTBA receipt should arrive within **15 business days**; if it does not, the form says you may email **rtba@justice.vic.gov.au** or call **1300 137 164**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The retrieved document does not expressly resolve whether this prohibits the particular card surcharge you describe, as opposed to a fee for establishing or using the facility.

[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2026-10/97-109aa115-authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** provide a clear answer that makes the result depend on whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent. Section 42 applies to the rental provider or agent’s obligation to provide a fee-free method and disclose costs, while section 51(3) refers broadly to **“a person”**. ## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent, in writing:

2. **Is the bank-transfer option genuinely available without any fee?**
3. **Was the fee disclosed before you consented to use the card method?**
4. **Is the fee for using the electronic payment facility, or only a separately identified third-party transaction surcharge?**

If the bank-transfer method is not reasonably available, or the fee was not disclosed beforehand, you can raise that with the agent and refer to **sections 42(4) and 42(7)** of **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111**. question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

On **8 November 2022**, the applicable documents were:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101**—in force from 7 September 2022; and  
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002**—in force from 1 June 2022. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental agreement must state the rental provider’s details and, where applicable, the agent’s details. The prescribed agreement says the rental provider must notify the renter **within 7 days** if those details change. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

Rent is payable in the manner specified in the agreement. The rental provider and renter may change that payment method **by agreement**. A fee-free payment method—apart from your own bank or account fees—must remain reasonably available, and the provider must allow Centrepay and any prescribed payment method. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The bond is separate from rent. The rental provider or agent must lodge it with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) **within 10 business days** of receiving it, and the RTBA must send you a receipt. If you have not received the receipt within **15 business days**, you may notify the Authority. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** prescribe a particular bank-account verification process for a change from agency management to owner management.

## What you can do or ask before paying

1. **Check your signed lease** for the named rental provider, agent, payment method and payment details. Ask the agency and owner in writing to confirm:
   - the owner’s full name and contact details;
   - that the agency’s management has ended;
   - the date the change takes effect; and
   - that the new account is the account for rent under your existing agreement.  
   The owner’s changed details should be provided consistently with the agreement’s required information. [[5]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Do not treat the new bank details as automatically replacing the lease terms.** Ask for written confirmation that you agree to the changed payment method, because the Act says the payment method may be changed by agreement. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Independently verify the account** with the agency using contact details already in your lease or earlier correspondence—not only by replying to the message containing the new details. The retrieved documents do not say exactly how identity or bank details must be verified, so this is a sensible precaution rather than a specific statutory procedure.

4. **Ask for a rent receipt** after payment. If you request a written receipt when paying electronically, the recipient must provide it within **5 business days**; the receipt must identify you and the premises, date, payment period, amount and that it is rent. [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Check your bond status separately.** Confirm that you received the RTBA receipt and that the bond is recorded under the correct rental provider and premises. If no receipt arrives within 15 business days of payment, notify the Authority. [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088**, incorporating amendments as at **2 July 2019**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Because you had **not yet entered into possession**, section 226 allowed you to terminate the tenancy by giving the landlord a notice of termination if the premises:

- were **not in good repair**;
- were **unfit for human habitation**;
- were unsafe;
- were not legally available or otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had a duty to maintain the premises in **good repair**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The Act treated a fault or damage making premises unsafe or insecure as an **urgent repair**, including mould or damp caused by, or related to, the building structure. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Cancel/terminate before moving in:**  
   Give the landlord written notice under **section 226**, stating that you have not entered possession and that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for habitation, or are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not state that merely receiving the keys prevents you using section 226; the stated condition is that you have **not entered into possession**. [[9]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for repairs:**  
   Notify the landlord in writing and request immediate repairs. If the mould or damp is structural and makes the premises unsafe or insecure, it may be an urgent repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) If the landlord does not act, you may arrange urgent repairs after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them; the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or **$1,000, whichever is less**, after you give **14 days’ written notice** of the repairs and cost. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) You may instead apply to the Tribunal for urgent-repair orders if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs exceed $1,000, or the landlord refuses to pay; the Tribunal must hear that application within **2 business days**. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

   For non-urgent repairs, give written notice. If they are not done within **14 days**, you may ask the Director to investigate and then apply to the Tribunal for a repair order. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Ask for lower rent:**  
   The retrieved documents do **not** provide a general right, on these facts, to unilaterally reduce the rent. They do provide a process to apply to the Tribunal for permission to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account** after notice requiring repairs has been given and the landlord has failed to comply. [[6]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Do not simply stop paying rent without an order.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

On **8 November 2022**, the applicable documents were:

- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, **Authorised Version 101**, in force from **7 September 2022** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) The provider or agent must also make a payment method available that does not incur additional costs apart from your own bank or account fees, and must permit Centrepay or any prescribed payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The standard agreement records the provider’s payment methods and payment details, and says the renter is entitled to a receipt for rent paid. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) If you request a written receipt for an electronic payment when you make it, the person receiving the rent must provide it within **5 business days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The bond is separate from rent: the provider or agent must lodge it with the RTBA within **10 business days** of receiving it, and the RTBA should send you a receipt. If you do not receive that receipt within **15 business days**, you may contact the RTBA by email or telephone. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The documents **do not state** that an agent’s change to the owner’s management automatically changes the payment details, nor do they specify a particular bank-account verification process.

Confirm that the proposed payment method complies with the agreement and does not impose extra payment costs; any costs of a particular electronic payment method must be explained before you agree to use it. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
5. Check your **RTBA bond receipt**. If you have not received it within 15 business days of paying the bond, contact the RTBA using the details in the regulations. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
6. Keep the request, your verification, the lease, and proof of payment, and request a rent receipt after paying. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 111)** and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 005)**, which were in force on January 15, 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf):

### What the law says
*   **Right to a fee-free method:** The landlord or their agent must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs **no additional costs** (other than your own bank's standard account fees) is reasonably available to you at all times [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 
*   **Mandatory cost disclosure:** Before you consent to use any specific payment method, the landlord or agent must give you clear information about any costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees and electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
*   **Regulatory confirmation:** The standard tenancy agreement explicitly notes that providers must permit a fee-free payment method and allow the use of Centrepay or other electronic funds transfers [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

### Can the app charge you the card fee?
Yes, but only under strict conditions:
1.  **You cannot be forced to pay it.** Because your landlord/agent has already provided a manual bank transfer option with no fee, they are legally meeting their obligation to provide a reasonably available fee-free method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 
2.  **It must be transparent.** The landlord or agent was required to inform you of the card fee *before* you agreed to use that payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3.  **It is voluntary.** Since a free alternative exists, you are not legally obligated to pay the card fee. You can simply decline the card option and use the manual bank transfer instead.

### Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent?
No, it does not change your legal rights:
*   The law focuses on the **cost incurred by you** (categorized as "third party transaction fees" or "electronic payment facility fees") rather than who pockets the money [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 
*   Whether the fee is retained by the app provider to cover processing costs or passed through by the agent, your statutory right to a fee-free payment method remains identical [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   *Practical distinction:* If the agent is illegally demanding you pay a card fee while denying you the free option, the breach falls on the landlord/agent under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If the app charges a standard processing fee for a service you voluntarily selected, that is a separate commercial arrangement between you and the app provider.

### What you can do
*   **Use the free option:** Simply pay via the manual bank transfer to avoid the fee entirely.
*   **Report non-compliance:** If your landlord or agent pressures you into using card payments or refuses to accept the fee-free bank transfer, they are breaching their legal obligations [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). You can lodge a complaint with Consumer Affairs Victoria or apply to VCAT for a compliance order.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?

**Asking for repairs:** 
Yes, you can request urgent repairs. Under the law at that time, "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" is explicitly classified as an **urgent repair** because it makes the rented premises unsafe or insecure [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 

**Cancelling the lease or asking for lower rent:**
The provided documents do not contain information on whether you can cancel your lease or request a rent reduction in this situation.

It covers urgent repairs for mould and damp, but it never mentions the landlord's duty to keep the premises in good repair under s 68.
