The answer names the Act as 'Authorised Version No. 111, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025' (link 97-109aa111) and the Regulations as 'the version dated 25 November 2025' (link 21-3sra005, i.e. version 005), and every rule it applies is cited to one of these in-force versions.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the documents, your landlord or agent probably can't make you pay a card fee when a fee-free option, such as bank transfer, is reasonably available. The documents don't say whether the fee goes to the app company or the agent, and that difference doesn't appear to change the rule.

**Versions in force:** On 15 January 2026, the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf, dated 25 November 2025, version 111) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf, dated 25 November 2025, version 005) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) were both in force. I'm relying on the version numbers in the documents' metadata.

**What the law says**

- The provider or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Before you agree to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, including "third party transaction fees" and "any other electronic payment facility fees" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The provider must allow payment by Centrepay and by a prescribed method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The prescribed method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- A term in a residential rental agreement that requires the renter to pay rent in advance by a payment method that has additional costs (other than bank or account fees) is a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Schedule 1 of the regulations notes that the provider "must permit at least one fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

The documents don't distinguish between a fee paid to the app company and one paid to the agent. The obligations in section 42(4) fall on the provider "or that person's agent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address whether an app company acting for the agent changes this. I can't confirm that from these documents.

**A rule that doesn't yet apply:** Regulation 21C bans rent payment fees, except payment surcharges permitted under another Act, but it "has effect on and after 31 March 2026" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). It is not in force on 15 January 2026. The documents also don't include the text of section 51A of the Act, which it refers to [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**What you can do**

- Ask the provider or agent to confirm in writing that a no-fee method, such as bank transfer, is available, and that you can use it without paying the card fee.
- Ask for the cost information the law requires them to give you before you consent to the card option [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- If you pay by bank transfer, you can request a written receipt. For a payment not made in person, it must be given "within 5 business days of receiving the payment" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't describe how to make a complaint or what the Tribunal process is, so I can't advise on those steps from these sources.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. For the first, the answer quotes the duty to make 'a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account)' reasonably available, and says the card fee can't be forced 'when a fee-free option, such as bank transfer, is reasonably available.' For the second, it says reg 21C 'has effect on and after 31 March 2026' and 'is not in force on 15 January 2026.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer does not claim the card fee is already banned, since it says reg 21C 'has effect on and after 31 March 2026' and 'is not in force on 15 January 2026', and it affirms a fee-free rule exists, quoting that the provider 'must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs ... is reasonably available to the renter'.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf, dated 25 November 2025, version 111' (link 97-109aa111) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as 'rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf, dated 25 November 2025, version 005' (link 21-3sra005), both in force on 15 January 2026, and it says reg 21C is not yet in force rather than applying it.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 15 October 2019, you can likely cancel if you haven't moved in, and you can require repairs. The documents don't give you a right to reduce rent for these defects.

**Governing version:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088 (file rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf, in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019), applies on your date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). It uses the newer terms "residential rental provider" (landlord) and "renter" (tenant) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

---

### What the law says

- **Condition on move-in:** The provider must ensure the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition on the agreed day you enter occupation. If they aren't, you are not required to move in, and you don't have to pay rent for the period before you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This section is about cleanliness, so it doesn't clearly cover damp or rot.
- **Minimum standards:** The provider must ensure the premises comply with prescribed rental minimum standards on or before the day you enter occupation (penalty: 60 penalty units for an individual, 300 for a body corporate). If they don't comply on or just after that day, you may request urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents do not include the content of these standards.
- **Good repair:** The provider must keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit and suitable for occupation. This applies even if you knew of the disrepair before moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Mould and damp:** "Urgent repairs" includes "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure," and any fault that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether rotting timber counts as unsafe.

---

### What you can do

**1. Cancel**
- If you have not entered possession and you give the landlord notice of termination on the ground that the premises are not in good repair or are unfit for human habitation, the tenancy terminates [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Check first whether picking up the keys counts as taking possession. If it does, this route may not apply.
- The documents don't state a notice period for this termination.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Notify in writing:** Give written notice as soon as practicable after you become aware of the damage or breakdown [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you receive a condition report, it counts as notice of any defects it states [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you were not given one, you may complete one and give it to the provider within the period between inspecting the premises and 5 business days after moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** If you have taken reasonable steps to get the provider to repair immediately and they can't, you may arrange the repairs. The provider must reimburse the reasonable cost within 7 days after written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs at the Tribunal (VCAT):** You can apply if you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than the prescribed amount, or the provider refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Non-urgent repairs:** If repairs aren't done within 14 days after your written notice, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring specified repairs. The Tribunal must hear the application within 7 days and may order that a suitably qualified person carry out the work [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account:** If you have given notice and the provider has failed to carry out repairs, you may apply for an order that your rent be paid into the Rent Special Account. The Tribunal must make the order unless the provider shows financial hardship [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents do not contain a provision allowing you to reduce rent because of these defects.
- The closest provisions are the no-rent-before-move-in rule described above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) and the Director's power to investigate rent that is excessive, which is tied to reduced services or a proposed rent increase [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Neither clearly provides a rent reduction in your situation.
- Holding rent in the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) is not a reduction.

---

**Next steps:** Put your complaint in writing now, with photos, and keep a copy. Then decide whether to cancel or require repairs, and consider taking advice from VCAT or Consumer Affairs Victoria before acting. This summary is based only on the Act text retrieved and is not legal advice.

(2) The repair duty is stated: 'The provider must keep the premises in good repair and reasonably fit and suitable for occupation.' question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** The retrieved documents don't say how to verify a bank account or spot a payment scam. They do set rules on rent payment methods, notice of changed landlord details, receipts, and bond. Both documents were in force on 8 November 2022.

**Which law applies**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version 101 (in force from 7 September 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, Authorised Version 002 (in force from 1 June 2022) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What the law says**
- **Payment method:** The prescribed payment method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The standard form says the rental provider must permit at least one fee-free payment method (other than the renter's own bank fees) and must allow Centrepay or another electronic transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). A term requiring rent to be paid by a method that carries additional costs (other than bank or account fees) is a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Change of details:** The rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the provider or agent details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Contact-detail changes must be notified in writing immediately [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts:** The renter is entitled to a receipt confirming rent payment [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond:** The provider or agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days of receiving it [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If the renter has no RTBA receipt within 15 business days of paying, they may contact the RTBA [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the provider's rights and duties are transferred to another person, the provider and that person must notify the RTBA within 5 days, and the provider must give the renter a copy of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**What to check before paying the new account**
1. **Written notice of the change** from the owner or agent, with the owner's full name and address for service, and contact details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Payment method:** Confirm the new arrangement is a fee-free method (apart from your own bank fees), or Centrepay or electronic transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Bond status:** Confirm your bond was lodged with the RTBA and that you have the bond lodgment form copy [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the owner is taking over the agreement, ask whether the RTBA notice under the transfer rules has been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Receipts:** Make sure you will receive a receipt for each rent payment [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**What you can ask for or do**
- Ask the agent or owner for the change in writing and the new provider details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- Ask for confirmation that the new payment method carries no extra cost to you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- If you have no RTBA receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, contact the RTBA by email at rtba@justice.vic.gov.au [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The two forms list different RTBA phone numbers (1300 137 164 and 1300 13 71 64), so check the current number before calling [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

**Not covered by these documents:** How to verify that a bank account belongs to the owner, how to recognise payment fraud, and whether an owner can take over rent collection from an agent without a new agreement. If you're unsure, check with Consumer Affairs Victoria before transferring money.

must-mention.reason: No. The third point is missing. The answer never says that a change to how or where rent is paid is made by agreement under the lease (s 42). It even lists whether the owner can take over rent collection without a new agreement as 'not covered'. It also never tells the renter to confirm the new bank details through a known contact before paying, and asking 'the agent or owner for the change in writing' does not cover that. The answer also omits the emergency repairs number from the s 66 notice requirements.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter may stop paying rent, and it asserts that notice is required, stating "The rental provider must notify the renter within 7 days if the provider or agent details change" and "Contact-detail changes must be notified in writing immediately."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "Authorised Version 101 (in force from 7 September 2022)" with the link 97-109aa101, which is the required document and version. The only other document it relies on is the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, "Authorised Version 002 (in force from 1 June 2022)" (21-3sra002), which was also in force on 8 November 2022. No rule is drawn from an earlier or later version.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**What the law says**

Under the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Version 111, in force from 25 November 2025) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), the provider must ensure every smoke alarm is correctly installed and working, has batteries, and is tested at least once every 12 months [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The provider can enter to carry out that duty [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The entry rules are:

- **Hours:** Entry is allowed at any time agreed with the renter if the renter consented within the previous 7 days. Otherwise, entry is allowed between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, with at least 24 hours' notice [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice:** The notice must be in writing, state why the provider wants to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Manner:** The provider must enter in a reasonable manner and must not stay longer than necessary without your consent [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Your duty:** A renter must permit entry that complies with the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Regulations (Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025) say the renter must allow entry where the provider has followed proper procedure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be there yourself?**

The retrieved documents do not say whether you must be personally present. They only set out the hours, notice and manner rules above, and your duty to allow entry that follows them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I can't confirm from these sources whether you have to be home.

**Can they charge you $90?**

The documents do not cover this. Nothing I retrieved addresses a rebooking fee for a missed or rescheduled inspection. The only fee provisions I found are about consent to assignment or sub-letting [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and rental application and rent payment fees, which only take effect on 31 March 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Neither applies here, so I can't say whether the $90 fee is lawful.

**Points to raise with your agent**

- The Act allows entry between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on non-public-holiday days, so the 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. window is narrower than the statute [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A different time may still be agreed with you [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Ask for the entry notice in writing, stating the reason for entry, with at least 24 hours' notice, and delivered in the way the Act requires [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Ask the agent to put the $90 charge in writing and identify the provision that authorises it. If you disagree, you can check guidance at the Consumer Affairs Victoria renting website, which the Regulations refer to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can also ask VCAT for an order limiting when entry may occur [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No: the answer leaves the point that the renter does not have to be present unresolved, saying "I can't confirm from these sources whether you have to be home," so a reader cannot tell which way it falls. It also never says the agent can enter with the inspector on proper notice.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must be home or must pay the $90; it says "I can't confirm from these sources whether you have to be home" and "I can't say whether the $90 fee is lawful."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as "Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Version 111, in force from 25 November 2025)" with link 97-109aa111, and the Regulations as "Version 005, in force from 25 November 2025" with link 21-3sra005. Both are the versions in force on 3 December 2025, and it relies on no other version for any rule it applies.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the rules in force on 15 January 2026, your landlord or agent must make a no-extra-cost payment method reasonably available, and your bank transfer option may satisfy that. Whether the app can lawfully keep a card fee is less clear, because the key rule doesn't take effect until 31 March 2026. The documents don't say whether the app's fee is banned before then.

**Which law applies:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 111, in force 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021, version 005, in force 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) both apply on 15 January 2026.

**What the law says**

- **Fee-free option must be available:** A landlord or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 penalty units for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed:** The landlord or agent must give information about costs, including third-party transaction fees, "before the renter consents to use the payment method" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Fees charged by a business:** Section 51A bars a business other than the landlord, the agent, or a deposit-taking institution from demanding or receiving a fee for a "prescribed matter" in relation to paying rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The regulations list prescribed matters, including "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). However, that regulation "has effect on and after 31 March 2026" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't show a prescribed matter covering rent payment fees on 15 January 2026, so they don't confirm that the app's card fee is banned yet.
- **Prohibited term:** A lease term requiring rent to be paid in advance by a method with additional costs (other than bank or account fees) is a prescribed prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't state when this provision started.

**Does it matter who gets the fee?**

Yes, but mainly for the fee ban, not the no-extra-cost rule:

- **If the app company keeps it:** The app is not one of the people exempt under section 51A(2) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), so the app's fee falls under the section 51A ban once a prescribed matter covers it, which is from 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **If the agent takes it:** Agents are exempt from section 51A(1) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the agent still must make a fee-free method available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and must disclose costs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty for breaching that duty is the same whoever receives the money.

The documents don't define "payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act," so I can't say which surcharges are permitted.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the bank transfer option in writing.** It is fee-free apart from your own bank fees, so it appears to satisfy the requirement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't address whether a slower method is "reasonably available," so that point is unresolved.
2. **Ask for the cost details before you choose a payment method.** The landlord or agent must give this information before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for a receipt.** If you request one when paying electronically, it must be provided within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask whether the lease permits a method change.** Payment method can be changed by agreement between you and the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover dispute procedures or how to enforce these rules, so please check with Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT before taking formal action.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On the first, the answer says a landlord or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available," and that the fee-free bank transfer "appears to satisfy the requirement." The second point is the harder one: the answer says "the key rule doesn't take effect until 31 March 2026" and that the app's fee falls under the section 51A ban "once a prescribed matter covers it, which is from 31 March 2026," which clearly conveys that the fee ban is not yet in effect on 15 January 2026.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the output does not say the card fee is already banned. It states the regulation "has effect on and after 31 March 2026" and that the documents "don't confirm that the app's card fee is banned yet." It also affirms the fee-free rule: the landlord or agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs... is reasonably available to the renter."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 111, in force 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026)' and 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (S.R. No. 3/2021, version 005, in force 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026)', and it relies only on those versions while correctly treating the rent-payment prescribed matter as taking effect on 31 March 2026 rather than applying it as current law.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the version of the Act in force on 15 October 2019, you can likely give notice to end the lease, arrange urgent repairs or seek a repair order, and in some cases withhold rent. The documents do not give a clear right to a rent reduction for these defects.

**Governing law:** The *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (No. 109 of 1997), Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019, applies on your date. It was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The document also contains amendment text in its endnotes that uses "residential rental provider" and "renter" terms, but it does not say when that text commences. I have relied on the body of the Act. The Act states that references to landlords and tenants are read as references to residential rental providers and renters [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### What the law says

- **Repairs duty:** A landlord must ensure rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Condition at move-in:** A landlord must ensure that, on the agreed day you enter occupation, the premises are vacant and reasonably clean. You are not required to move into premises that do not comply, and you need not pay rent for the period before you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Condition report:** If you pay a bond, the landlord must give you two copies of a condition report before you enter occupation, specifying the state of repair. You must return a signed copy within 3 business days of moving in, and you can endorse that you disagree with any part of it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). A signed report is conclusive evidence of state of repair, unless the defect could not reasonably have been discovered on inspection or you disagree with it under an endorsement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### Your options

**1. Cancel (end the agreement)**
- If you have not entered into possession, the tenancy terminates if you give the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises "are not in good repair" or "are unfit for human habitation" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If you have moved in, you may give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation. The termination date may be the date the notice is given or a later date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The documents do not define "entered into possession," so it is unclear whether picking up the keys counts. Take advice on this point.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Notify in writing:** You must give the landlord written notice of non-urgent repairs. If they are not carried out within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** You may arrange urgent repairs if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them immediately and they cannot or will not. You must give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repair definition:** Urgent repairs include any fault or damage that makes the premises unsafe or insecure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The body text does not expressly list damp or mould. The endnote amendment that adds "presence of mould or damp" is not confirmed as in force by the documents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Tribunal:** You may apply to VCAT (the Tribunal) for an order requiring specified repairs. For non-urgent repairs, you must apply within 60 days of receiving the Director's report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For urgent repairs, the Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents do not contain a general right to reduce rent for initial defects.
- The closest provision is the excessive rent process. The Tribunal must declare rent excessive if it is more than a tenant should reasonably pay, having regard to, among other things, the "state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This process is framed around rent increases and reduced services, so its application to a new lease is uncertain [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If you have given a repair notice and the landlord has failed to comply, you may apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This is a pressure tool, not a reduction.
- Rent is not payable for any period before you actually move in if the premises do not comply with the move-in duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### Practical steps

1. Put your complaint in writing now, listing the damp, mould and rotting timber.
2. Check the condition report, if one has been given. Endorse any disagreement within 3 business days of moving in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
3. Photograph everything.
4. Keep records of all communication and costs.

**Not covered by the documents:** The documents do not cover whether the lease can be cancelled without other consequences, or whether a rent reduction is available for initial defects. This is general information based only on the retrieved text, not legal advice. Consider speaking to Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy legal service.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't say how to verify a bank account, and they don't address payment fraud. They do set out rules on how rent may be paid and changed, and on the bond and receipts, which you can check before paying.

**What the law says**

- Where the rent is payable depends on the agreement. Rent is payable at the place the agreement specifies, or at the premises if none is specified, and otherwise in the manner the agreement specifies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The manner of payment can change only by agreement. The rental provider and renter, "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). So a unilateral notice of new bank details is not, on the text, a change you're bound by.
- Before you agree to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using it, such as third-party transaction fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- The provider or agent must make a no-extra-cost payment method reasonably available, other than your own bank or account fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). They must also permit payment by Centrepay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- If the new owner or agent changes, the standard lease form requires the rental provider to notify the renter within 7 days if agent details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- Any payment you make must be receipted. For a payment not made in person, a receipt must be given within 5 business days if you request one. The receipt must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**What to check and ask before paying**

1. **Ask for the change in writing and confirm the payment method is agreed.** Because changing the payment manner requires agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), you can decline to pay into a new account until you have agreed to the change.
2. **Ask about fees.** Ask whether any fees apply to the new account or method, since the provider must give you that information before you consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Confirm who the landlord and agent are.** The lease form requires notice within 7 days of changes to agent details [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Check that the person sending the new details is the owner named on your agreement or an authorised agent. An agent must produce evidence of their authorisation if the Bond Authority asks [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Check the bond.** The provider or agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 10 business days of receiving it. The RTBA sends a receipt. If you have not received one within 15 business days of paying, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Confirm the bond is lodged before the handover.
5. **Keep records.** Keep receipts for every rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**What the documents don't cover**

- They don't say whether a switch from an agency to owner-management counts as a transfer of the landlord's rights. If it does, the owner must notify the Bond Authority within 5 days and give you a copy of the notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether that applies here, so you may wish to ask.
- They don't set out how to verify a bank account, and they don't address scams. Confirming the new details with the owner or agent through contact information you already have is a practical step, but it is my suggestion, not something the documents require.

**Sources**
- [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101 (rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf), in force from 7 September 2022.
- [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf) Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002 (rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf), in force from 1 June 2022.

It never says the landlord must give written notice of their full name, address for service and an emergency repairs number. question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**What the law says (as at 3 December 2025)**

The Residential Tenancies Act 1997 is in Authorised Version No. 111, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 are in version 005 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 3 December 2025.

- **Renter's duty:** A renter must permit a person exercising a right of entry under the Act to enter the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Smoke alarm duty:** The landlord must ensure each smoke alarm is tested at least once every 12 months, in line with the manufacturer's instructions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm check can therefore be a lawful reason for entry.
- **Timing and notice:** For this purpose, entry is allowed at any time between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, if at least 24 hours' notice has been given [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entry can also happen at any time the renter agrees, if the renter consented within 7 days before the entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Notice requirements:** The notice must be in writing, state why the landlord or agent wants to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Manner of entry:** The person entering must act reasonably and must not stay longer than necessary [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be there yourself?**

The documents do not say whether the renter must be personally present. They say the renter must *permit* lawful entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), and they don't address whether the renter has to be home. If you can't be there, the documents don't give a rule either way, so I can't confirm whether your presence is required.

**Can they charge $90 to rebook?**

The documents contain no provision allowing a rebooking fee. They also don't mention the agent's 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. window. The Act's entry window is 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A landlord or agent must not demand or accept payment from a renter who has failed to comply with the agreement or the Act, other than rent or an amount or penalty provided for in the Act [[4]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I haven't retrieved the text of section 51 ("Certain charges prohibited"), so I can't confirm whether it covers this fee. I also can't tell from the documents whether the $90 appears in your tenancy agreement.

**What you can do or ask**

1. **Ask for the notice in writing.** It must state why entry is needed, be in writing, and be given by post or personally delivered between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Check that it gives at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
2. **Propose a time.** Entry at an agreed time is allowed if you consented within 7 days before the entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Ask for the legal basis of the $90 fee in writing.** The documents don't show any authority for it.
4. **Apply to VCAT to limit entry.** You may apply to the Tribunal for an order specifying or limiting the days, times and purposes of entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
5. **Seek protection if entry breaks the rules.** You may apply to the Tribunal for an order restraining entry for a specified period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), or for compensation if damage is caused to your goods during entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
6. **Get more information.** The regulations refer to consumer.vic.gov.au/renting for more information [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing: the answer never says the renter does not have to be present, nor that the agent can enter with the inspector on proper notice. It hedges with "the documents don't give a rule either way, so I can't confirm whether your presence is required," which leaves a reader unable to tell which way the point falls.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must be home or must pay the fee: on presence it says "the documents don't give a rule either way, so I can't confirm whether your presence is required," and on the fee it says "The documents contain no provision allowing a rebooking fee" and "don't show any authority for it."

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Act as "Authorised Version No. 111, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025" (link 97-109aa111) and the Regulations as "version 005" (link 21-3sra005), and every rule it applies is cited to one of these in-force versions, with no reliance on any other version.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not as a standing card fee, but the answer depends on whether the fee is a charge for using an electronic payment facility, and on whether the renter's tenancy agreement sets the payment method. The fee recipient matters less than you might expect.

**What the law says (as at 15 January 2026)**

I'm applying the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (Authorised Version No. 111, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (Authorised Version No. 005, in force from 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

- **No charge for electronic payment facilities:** A person must not demand or receive a charge from a renter for the "establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent." The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This is not limited to the agent, so it could reach the app company if the fee is a charge for using the payment facility.
- **A free method must be available:** The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank or account fees) is reasonably available to the renter. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person or 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Costs must be disclosed:** The provider or agent must tell the renter about any costs, including third-party transaction fees, before the renter consents to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Bank transfer counts as a permitted method:** The prescribed payment method is electronic funds transfer [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). A manual bank transfer should fit this.
- **Prohibited terms:** A term in the agreement requiring rent to be paid in advance by a method that requires additional costs (other than bank or account fees) is a prescribed prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**Fee recipient:** The provider and agent are covered by the rules above. The general prohibition on rent-payment fees for businesses (s 51A) exempts the provider and agent but applies to other businesses [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). However, the regulation that prescribes which fees are caught (reg 21C) only takes effect on 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). So on 15 January 2026, the documents do not show a specific prohibition on the app company's fee under s 51A. The documents also don't say whether the app company is a separate "business" for this purpose.

**What you can do or ask**

1. Ask the agent or provider in writing to confirm the fee-free methods they accept, and to disclose the card fee amount and who receives it.
2. Point out that a fee-free method must be "reasonably available" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Ask whether a slower bank transfer meets that standard. The documents don't define "reasonably available," so this is a judgement call.
3. Check your agreement for a clause requiring card payment or allowing fees. Such a clause may be a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
4. If the agent or provider refuses, you can seek help from Consumer Affairs Victoria or VCAT. The documents don't cover those processes, so check current guidance.

**Gaps in the documents:**
- They don't say whether the app company's fee is caught by s 51(3) in practice, or how "reasonably available" should be applied to a slower method.
- Reg 21C, which lists prohibited rent-payment fees, applies from 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). It isn't in force yet on 15 January 2026.
- The Regulations version I reviewed expires on 9 February 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), so a later version may apply to any dispute after that date. The documents don't include it.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. On point 1, the answer says a no-extra-cost method must be 'reasonably available' and that 'A manual bank transfer should fit this', while noting that whether the slower transfer meets that standard 'is a judgement call', which conveys that it may satisfy the requirement. On point 2, it states that 'reg 21C ... only takes effect on 31 March 2026' and 'isn't in force yet on 15 January 2026.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not claim the fee is already banned under s 51A or reg 21C, stating that reg 21C "only takes effect on 31 March 2026" and that "on 15 January 2026, the documents do not show a specific prohibition on the app company's fee under s 51A". It also affirms that "a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs... is reasonably available to the renter" is required.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version No. 111, in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026)' and the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version No. 005, in force from 25 November 2025 to 9 February 2026)', both in force on 15 January 2026. It treats reg 21C only as not yet in effect and does not apply rules from any other version.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Governing version:** The Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088 (incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019), is the version in force on 15 October 2019. Its metadata gives an in-force period of 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **Condition on move-in day:** The landlord must ensure that on the day you are to move in, the premises are vacant and reasonably clean. If they are not, you are not required to move in, and you do not have to pay rent from the agreed move-in day until the day you actually move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 65).
- **Repair duty:** The landlord must ensure the premises are "maintained in good repair" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 68(1)).
- **Damp and mould:** The amendment text in the endnotes adds "the presence of mould or damp caused by or related to the building structure" to the definition of urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The retrieved documents do not confirm when that amendment took effect, so check whether it applied on 15 October 2019.

## Can you cancel?

The retrieved material does not answer this. The table of provisions lists "Termination by tenant before possession" (s 226) and "Premises destroyed or unfit for habitation" (s 238) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), but I could not retrieve their text. I can't confirm a right to cancel from these documents. What I can say is that s 65 means you are not required to move in and owe no rent for the period before you actually move in, if the premises don't meet the move-in standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Can you ask for repairs?

Yes. The steps in the document are:

1. **Give written notice.** You must give the landlord written notice that repairs (other than urgent repairs) are needed. If the landlord does not carry them out within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 74).
2. **Urgent repairs.** If you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord to repair them immediately and cannot get them done, you may arrange the repairs yourself. You must give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost. The landlord must then reimburse the reasonable cost or $1,000, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 72). The endnote amendment changes the reimbursement period to 7 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), but I cannot confirm that it applied on 15 October 2019.
3. **Tribunal orders.** You can apply to the Tribunal for an urgent-repair order if you cannot meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $1,000, or the landlord refuses to pay. The Tribunal must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 73). For non-urgent repairs, you can apply within 60 days of receiving the Director's report [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 75). The Tribunal can order the landlord to carry out specified repairs within a specified time [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 76).
4. **Rent into the Rent Special Account.** After you have given repair notice and the landlord has failed to comply, you can apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into the Rent Special Account [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 77).

## Can you ask for lower rent?

Yes, but the route is a complaint or application about **excessive rent**. You may complain to the Director about excessive rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 45) or apply to the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 46). In deciding what rent is reasonable, the Tribunal must have regard to the state of repair and general condition of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 47(1)(b)). If the Tribunal makes an order, the landlord cannot require rent above the ordered amount for 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 47(4)), and the Tribunal may order a refund of the difference from the date you applied [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) (s 48).

## Summary and limits

- You are not required to move in until the premises are reasonably clean, and you pay no rent until you do [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can demand repairs in writing, then go to the Director or the Tribunal [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You can ask for a lower rent through the excessive-rent provisions [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The documents I retrieved do not show whether you can cancel the agreement, because the relevant termination provisions were not in the retrieved text.

This is general information based only on the retrieved Act, not legal advice. For a decision about cancelling or a dispute, get advice from the Director or the Tribunal.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Short answer:** Under the law in force on 8 November 2022, a change to how rent is paid needs your agreement, and the new method must meet the rules below. The documents I found don't say how to verify a bank account, so you'll need to confirm the details independently.

## What the law says

- **Change must be agreed.** The Act says that the rental provider and renter, "by agreement, may change the manner in which rent is payable" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The agent saying the owner will manage the property and has new bank details doesn't, on its face, change your agreement.
- **Payment place and method.** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, or at the rented premises if none is specified [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Where the agreement sets the payment manner, rent is payable in that manner [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **No extra costs.** The rental provider or their agent "must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on the renter's bank account) is reasonably available to the renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Cost information first.** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees and direct debit dishonour fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Centrepay.** The provider or agent must permit payment by Centrepay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **No post-dated cheques.** Rent cannot be required by post-dated cheque or other post-dated negotiable instrument [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Who counts as the provider.** The definition of "residential rental provider" includes an agent of the provider [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The agent's notice is therefore given on the owner's behalf, but the agreement and payment rules still apply.

## What the renter can check or ask

1. **Your consent.** Don't treat the agent's message as a change to your agreement. Ask for the change in writing and agree to it only if you accept it.
2. **Fees.** Ask whether the new account incurs any fee beyond your own bank fees, and ask for the cost information the Act requires before you agree [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Payment options.** Ask whether Centrepay and a fee-free method are available. The prescribed agreement form says the provider "must permit at least one fee-free (other than the renter's own bank fees) payment method and must allow the renter to use Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer" [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Receipts.** You are entitled to a receipt confirming rent payment [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If you pay without being in person, you can request a receipt at the time of payment, and it must be given within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The receipt must be signed and must state your name and the premises, the date of receipt, the period paid, the amount, and that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Bond.** Check the bond is lodged. The provider must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days after receiving it . The Authority must send a receipt within 7 days . If you don't receive a receipt within 15 business days of paying the bond, you may email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call 1300 137 164 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Change of owner or agent.** The prescribed form notes that the provider must tell the renter within 7 days if agent details change [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If the owner takes over the rights and duties under the agreement and a bond was paid, the owner and the new person must notify the Authority within 5 days, and the provider must give you a copy of the notice .

## What the documents don't cover

- How to verify that the bank account belongs to the owner, or how to spot payment fraud. Confirm the account details directly with the owner or the agent through contact details you already have, not through the new message.
- Whether the owner must be named on the account.

The bond lodgement and receipt point and the 'change by agreement, confirm through known contact details' point are both covered.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
## What the law says

On **3 December 2025**, the applicable document is **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version 111**, in force from 25 November 2025. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The rental provider must ensure smoke alarms are correctly installed, working, fitted with batteries, and tested at least every 12 months; mains-powered alarms must be tested, repaired or replaced by a suitably qualified person. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The Act’s prescribed agreement summary says the rental provider may enter to comply with duties under the Act, and that the renter must allow entry when the proper procedure has been followed. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) **These documents do not say that the renter personally must be home or personally let the inspector in.** They also do not specify that a smoke-alarm appointment must be on a weekday or between 10 am and 12:30 pm. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

**The documents do not contain any provision authorising a $90 rebooking fee for a smoke-alarm check.** They therefore do not establish that the agent can charge you that amount. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent in writing to:

- identify the legal basis for requiring **you personally** to attend;
- explain how access will be provided if you are absent, such as through the agent or another authorised person; and
- identify the legal or contractual basis for the **$90 fee**, including an itemised invoice or evidence of the actual cost.

You should still cooperate with a properly arranged inspection and allow lawful entry, but **on these documents alone, you do not have to be personally present, and the $90 charge is not supported by anything retrieved**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No. The answer says testing smoke alarms is the rental provider's duty and that the renter need not be personally present, but it never states that entry to carry out a duty requires at least 24 hours' written notice within 8 am to 6 pm, or that the seven days' notice given satisfies this.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer asserts neither failing claim: it says 'on these documents alone, you do not have to be personally present, and the $90 charge is not supported by anything retrieved', so it rejects both personal attendance and the obligation to pay the fee.
