The answer names "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111" and cites the Regulations through the link "21-3sra005-authorised.pdf", which the rubric accepts as naming version 005. It describes that document only as "the Act's prescribed agreement summary" rather than by its title, but it relies on no out-of-force version.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 January 2026**, the applicable legislation was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111** (in force from 25 November 2025 to 29 June 2026). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The applicable regulations were the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

- The rental provider or agent must make **reasonably available** a rent-payment method that has **no additional cost**, apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- They must tell you about costs—including **third-party transaction fees** and **electronic payment facility fees**—before you agree to use a particular payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- A person must not demand or receive a charge for establishing or using a direct-debit facility or **any other electronic payment facility** for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)
- The prescribed rental agreement form also states that the rental provider must permit a fee-free payment method and allow Centrepay or another form of electronic funds transfer. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

Therefore, the documents do **not** clearly say that every card surcharge is lawful merely because a free bank-transfer option exists. A fee charged for using the app’s card-payment facility may be prohibited under section 51(3), depending on whether it is a charge for using an electronic payment facility. The documents do not specifically define “card fee” or decide this exact app scenario. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

It does not necessarily matter whether the money goes to the agent or the app company: section 51(3) applies to **“a person”**, while the fee-free-payment obligation applies to the rental provider or agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) However, the documents do not expressly determine whether an independent app company is legally treated as the relevant payment-facility provider in this situation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

## What the renter can do or ask

Ask the agent or rental provider:

1. **What is the legal basis for the card fee?**
2. **Who receives it—the agent, rental provider, app company, card processor or bank?**
3. **Why is the fee not prohibited as a charge for using an electronic payment facility?**
4. **Why is the fee-free bank-transfer option reasonably available**, particularly if the app option is faster but the transfer is slower?

You can state that you choose the fee-free bank-transfer method and ask for written confirmation that it will be accepted without penalty. The renter agreement form expressly identifies bank deposit and other electronic payment methods as payment options and requires a fee-free method to be permitted. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

If the fee was not disclosed before you agreed to use the card method, raise that specifically, because the Act requires information about applicable payment-method costs to be given before consent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: No: the answer never says that the specific rent-payment fee ban (reg 21C) does not yet apply on 15 January 2026 and only starts on 31 March 2026, and it instead suggests section 51(3) may already prohibit the card fee.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the card fee is already banned under s 51A or reg 21C (it says only that the fee 'may be prohibited under section 51(3)'), and it affirms a fee-free rule, stating the rental provider 'must make reasonably available a rent-payment method that has no additional cost'.

version-cited.reason: Yes — the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, "Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111" and "Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005" (links 97-109aa111 and 21-3sra005), and relies on no earlier or later version.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law said on 15 October 2019

The applicable law was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019**. That version was in force on 15 October 2019. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider had to ensure that the premises were **in good repair** and in a **reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation**, regardless of whether the renter knew about the disrepair before entering into occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Damp, mould and rotting timber may therefore amount to a breach, depending on their extent and effect, but the retrieved documents do not define exactly when those particular defects make premises “unfit for human habitation.” [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The Act also contained a specific rule allowing a tenant to terminate before possession where the premises were, among other things, **not in good repair, unfit for human habitation, unsafe, or otherwise unavailable for occupation**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The retrieved extract does not include the section number or full operative wording of that provision, so I cannot state the required notice procedure more precisely from these documents.

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask to cancel/terminate immediately.**  
   Write to the rental provider or agent, describe the damp, mould and rotten timber, attach photographs or reports, and say you seek termination because the premises are not in good repair and/or are unfit for occupation. The Act provides a termination route for premises in those conditions. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for repairs.**  
   The rental provider must arrange for the premises to be put and kept in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For non-urgent repairs, give written notice. If the repairs are not done within **14 days**, you may apply to the Director for an investigation; you may then apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs if satisfactory arrangements have not been made. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Do not move in while the premises are unsuitable.**  
   The law expressly says a tenant is not required to enter into occupation of premises that do not meet the statutory provision about being vacant and reasonably clean. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved documents do not clearly state whether simply collecting the keys counts as “entering into possession” for the termination-before-possession provision.

4. **Ask for lower rent, but the documents do not establish an automatic right to a rent reduction.**  
   You can ask the rental provider to agree to a lower rent if you are willing to accept the premises after repairs or with reduced amenity. The retrieved provisions instead provide for repair orders, compensation in an appropriate Tribunal proceeding, and—after notice of required repairs—an application to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account**; they do not state a general right to unilaterally reduce the agreed rent. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Do not simply stop paying rent without an order or agreement.**  
   The Act provides a specific Tribunal process for paying rent into the Rent Special Account where repairs have been notified and the rental provider has failed to comply. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

Keep the keys, lease, inspection/condition report, photographs, messages and any building or health report. The retrieved documents do not say whether you can recover the bond or moving-related costs on these facts.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer covers the termination right before possession, the landlord's good-repair duty, and the disrepair-versus-unclean distinction with photos as evidence, but it is missing the urgent-repairs point: it describes only non-urgent repairs with the 14-day process and never says that serious damage making the home unsafe can be treated as an urgent repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer never says the home must meet rental minimum standards or a mould and damp standard (it relies only on the 2019 Act's duty that the premises be 'in good repair and in a reasonably fit and suitable condition for occupation'), and it never says the renter must move in and pay rent (it advises 'Ask to cancel/terminate immediately' and 'Do not move in while the premises are unsuitable').

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019', and every rule it applies (repair duty, 14-day repair notice, Director investigation, Tribunal orders, Rent Special Account, termination before possession) is cited to the 97-109aa088 version in force on 15 October 2019, with no reliance on any other version.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

On **8 November 2022**, the applicable documents were:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101, in force from 7 September 2022** (“rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002, in force from 1 June 2022** (“rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf”). [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

The rental provider must give written notice of any change to the provider’s or agent’s contact information **within 7 days after the change**. If there is no longer an agent, the provider must give you the provider’s full name and address for service of documents, plus an emergency telephone number. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

If the rental provider has assigned or transferred their **rights and duties** under the agreement to another person, the provider and that person must notify the RTBA within **5 days**; the provider must also give you a copy of that notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

The documents do **not** specifically prescribe a procedure for verifying a changed rent bank account or say that rent must be paid into a particular type of account. They do say the rental provider must permit a fee-free payment method (apart from your own bank fees), allow electronic funds transfer, and give you a receipt confirming rent payment. question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
## What the law says

As at **Wednesday 3 December 2025**, the relevant documents are:

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The provider or agent may enter to carry out a duty under the Act, including this smoke-alarm duty, between **8 am and 6 pm on any day except a public holiday**, provided the required notice has been given. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

You must permit a person exercising that right of entry to enter, but the Act does **not** say that the renter must personally be at home or personally let the inspector in. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) It also says entry may be by the provider or agent **together with any persons necessary** to achieve its purpose. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

The retrieved documents do **not** state that a renter can be charged a **$90 rebooking fee** for not being home, nor do they provide a specific authority for that fee. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) Therefore, based only on these documents, I cannot say that the agent may lawfully charge it.

## What you can do or ask

You can tell the agent in writing that:

- you will permit the properly notified inspection;
- you do not accept that you must personally attend; and
- they should confirm how the inspector can obtain lawful access without you being present.

Ask the agent to identify the **legal or contractual basis** for the $90 fee and provide the relevant term or authority. The retrieved documents do not contain one. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

Also ask them to confirm that the appointment notice is written, states that the purpose is the smoke-alarm check, and gives the legally required notice. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 January 2026**, the applicable documents are:

- **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 111, dated 25 November 2025** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) On the documents retrieved, this means the card fee is not made lawful merely because it is described as an app or card-processing fee.

[[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) However, the retrieved documents do not expressly discuss the precise contractual relationship between an app company, agent and renter, so they do not provide a more detailed answer about the app company’s separate liability.

The prescribed payment method that must be permitted is **electronic funds transfer**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf) The standard rental agreement also states that at least one payment method must be fee-free, excluding only the renter’s own bank fees. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

- If they insist that you must pay the card fee, ask them to identify the legal basis for charging it, because the retrieved Act prohibits charges for establishing or using an electronic payment facility for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_, Authorised Version 088, dated 2 July 2019** (“AV 088”). [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord had to ensure that, on the agreed occupation day, the premises were **vacant and reasonably clean**. You were not required to enter into occupation if they did not meet that requirement, and you did not have to pay rent for the period before you actually entered into occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The landlord also had a continuing duty to maintain the premises in **good repair**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) Damp, mould and rotting timber may amount to repair or safety problems, but the retrieved document does not specifically classify those particular defects.

If you **had not entered into possession**, you could give the landlord a notice terminating the tenancy on the ground that the premises were **not in good repair**, **unfit for human habitation**, **unsafe**, **not vacant**, **not legally available as a residence**, or otherwise **unavailable for occupation**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask

1. **Ask to cancel by agreement.**  
   You can ask the landlord to agree in writing to terminate the tenancy; the Act expressly permits termination by agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) If the landlord agrees, obtain written confirmation about termination, keys, bond and any rent already paid.

2. **Give a statutory termination notice if you have not entered into possession.**  
   If you have not actually entered into possession, you can give a notice of termination relying on the relevant ground—for example, that the premises are not in good repair or are unavailable for occupation. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The document does not prescribe a particular notice period for section 226, so it does not provide a precise period to state here.

3. **Ask for repairs.**  
   Give the landlord written notice describing the damp, mould and rotting timber and request repairs. The landlord’s duty is to maintain the premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord does not act within **14 days** after written notice, the tenant may apply to the Director for an investigation; after receiving the Director’s report, the tenant may apply to the Tribunal for a repair order. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

4. **Ask for lower rent.**  
   You may ask the landlord to agree to a lower rent, but the retrieved document does not give an automatic right to a rent reduction merely because defects were found. The statutory excessive-rent process applies where services, facilities or other items have been reduced or withdrawn, or where the tenant has received a rent-increase notice; the state of repair and general condition of the premises are matters the Tribunal considers. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Do not simply stop paying rent without an order or agreement.**  
   The document provides a formal mechanism for applying to the Tribunal to pay rent into the **Rent Special Account** after notice requiring repairs has been given and the landlord has failed to comply; it does not state that a tenant may unilaterally withhold rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

**Practical position:** document the defects with photographs and written descriptions, notify the landlord immediately, and ask either for written cancellation and repayment of any money paid, or for a written repair plan. The retrieved document does not say whether merely collecting the keys counts as having “entered into possession”; that fact may affect whether section 226 is available.

must-mention.reason: No. The answer misses part of the second point: it never says that serious damage making the home unsafe can be an urgent repair. It only mentions the non-urgent repair process and says the document 'does not specifically classify those particular defects'. The other points are covered, including s 226 termination before possession for disrepair or unfitness, the landlord's good-repair duty with a repair request, and 'document the defects with photographs'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer relies only on the 2019 duties to deliver the premises 'vacant and reasonably clean' and keep them 'in good repair', and never claims the later rental minimum standards or mould and damp standard apply. It does not say the renter must move in and pay rent; instead it says 'You were not required to enter into occupation' and lists cancellation, repair and lower-rent options.

Every rule it applies (vacant and reasonably clean, good repair, s 226 termination before possession, the 14-day repair process through the Director, the Rent Special Account) is cited to that version and matches the pre-2021 Act, and it relies on no other version.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

On **Tuesday 8 November 2022**, the applicable document was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101 (in force 7 September 2022–23 May 2023)**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) The applicable regulations were the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

- The rent is payable at the place and in the manner specified in your residential rental agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider and renter may change the way rent is paid **by agreement**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf) Therefore, the documents do not say that an owner can unilaterally replace the agreed payment details merely because the agency will no longer manage the property. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- If the agency is no longer acting, the owner must give you written notice of the owner’s **full name and address for service of documents**, plus an emergency telephone number for urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- A change to the rental-provider or agent information must be notified in writing within **7 days** after the change. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- At least one rent-payment method must be available without additional costs other than your own bank or account fees, and you must be permitted to pay by **Centrepay** or another prescribed method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you should do or ask

Before paying the new account:

1. **Ask for written confirmation** that the agency’s authority has ended and that the owner is now the rental provider managing the tenancy. Ask for the owner’s full legal name, address for service, telephone number and urgent-repairs contact. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
2. **Check your signed lease**: see what payment method and payment details it specifies. The documents do not require you to accept a new bank account unless the payment method is changed by agreement. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
3. Ask the owner to confirm in writing that:
   - the new account is controlled by the owner or authorised rental provider;
   - the account is for rent for your specific premises; and
   - the amount and payment dates remain those in the lease.  
   The documents do not prescribe a particular bank-account verification process, so they do not say how you must independently verify the account.
4. If you agree to the new payment method, keep the written confirmation and proof of payment. The person receiving rent must provide a receipt if you request one when paying electronically; it must be provided within **5 business days** and state the renter, premises, date, period covered, amount and that it is rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
5. **Do not pay the bond again.** The provider or agent must lodge the bond with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within **10 business days** of receiving it, and the RTBA should send you a receipt within **7 days** of receiving it. If you have not received an RTBA receipt within **15 business days** after paying the bond, you may notify the Authority. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
6. If the new account or payment arrangement is unclear, ask the owner to resolve it before the due date while making clear in writing that you remain ready to pay rent under the lease. The retrieved documents do not state a specific procedure for disputing new bank details.

Point 1 (s 66): the answer says the owner must give written notice of their 'full name and address for service of documents, plus an emergency telephone number for urgent repairs', and that changes must be notified in writing 'within 7 days'. Point 2 (ss 406–407): it says the bond must be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority, that the RTBA should send a receipt, and that the renter may notify the Authority if no receipt arrives. - **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version No. 005, dated 25 November 2025**, in force on 15 January 2026. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

The rental provider or agent must make reasonably available **at least one rent-payment method with no additional cost**, apart from bank or account fees payable on the renter’s own bank account. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) A manual bank transfer with no fee appears to satisfy that requirement, even if it is slower. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

They must also tell you, **before you consent to use a payment method**, about costs you may incur, including third-party transaction fees and electronic-payment-facility fees. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

However, section 51(3) prohibits **“a person”** from demanding or receiving a charge for the establishment or use of direct-debit facilities or **any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The retrieved documents do not definitively say whether this particular card fee is legally characterised as such a prohibited charge or as a permissible third-party transaction fee. Therefore, they do not provide a conclusive yes-or-no answer about the card fee itself.

The newer prohibition on prescribed rent-payment fees does not resolve the position on 15 January: regulation 21C, including “rent payment”, only has effect **on and after 31 March 2026**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf)

It does **not appear to turn on who ultimately receives the fee**. Section 51(3) applies to “a person”, while the fee-free-method duty applies to the residential rental provider or that person’s agent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf) The documents do not contain an exception allowing the fee merely because it is paid to the app company rather than the agent.

## What you can do or ask

Ask the agent or provider, in writing:

1. **What is the legal basis and exact purpose of the card fee?**
2. Is it a fee for using an electronic payment facility, or a third-party transaction fee?
3. **Who receives it**—the app company, agent, or someone else?
4. Confirm that the no-fee bank-transfer option will remain reasonably available.
5. Ask why section 51(3) does not prohibit the fee if it is a charge for using an electronic payment facility for rent. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)

If the fee is charged by the app company directly, the retrieved documents do not state whether that company is the rental provider’s agent or otherwise determine the fee’s legality. On these documents alone, you should not assume that changing the recipient makes the fee lawful.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
## What the law says

On **15 October 2019**, the applicable document was **_Residential Tenancies Act 1997_ — Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019**. That version was in force from 2 July to 3 December 2019. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

A landlord had to ensure that, on the agreed occupation day, the premises were **vacant and reasonably clean**; a tenant was not required to enter premises that did not meet those requirements, and did not have to pay rent for the period before actually entering occupation if they did not. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The landlord also had to maintain the premises in **good repair**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

### Can you cancel?

Yes—**if you have not entered into possession**. You may give the landlord a notice terminating the tenancy if the premises:

- are **not in good repair**;
- are **unfit for human habitation**;
- are unsafe;
- are not vacant; or
- are otherwise unavailable for occupation. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

The Act does not state in the retrieved text whether merely collecting the keys amounts to entering into possession. Therefore, the documents do not resolve that factual issue. If you have not actually taken possession or moved in, section 226 is the relevant provision. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

If the premises are unfit for human habitation or have been rendered unsafe, a tenant may also give a notice of intention to vacate effective immediately or on a later date under section 238. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

### Can you ask for repairs?

Yes. The landlord must maintain the premises in good repair. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

You should give the landlord **written notice** describing the damp, mould and rotting timber and request repairs. For non-urgent repairs, if the landlord has not repaired them within **14 days**, you may apply to the Director for an investigation and report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) After receiving the report, you may apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring specified repairs; the application generally must be made within **60 days** of receiving the report. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

If the condition makes the premises **unsafe or insecure**, it falls within the Act’s definition of urgent repairs. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) In that case, after taking reasonable steps to have the landlord or agent act immediately, you may arrange the repairs if you cannot get them to do so; the landlord’s reimbursement obligation is limited to the reasonable cost or **$1,000**, whichever is less. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) You may instead apply to the Tribunal for urgent-repair orders where you cannot meet the cost, the cost exceeds **$1,000**, or the landlord refuses to pay. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)

### Can you ask for lower rent?

The retrieved documents do **not** provide a general right to an automatic rent reduction because of damp, mould or rotting timber.

They do provide a process for challenging **excessive rent**. You may apply to the Director if you consider the rent excessive because the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services, facilities or other items, or after receiving a rent-increase notice. The Tribunal may consider the premises’ state of repair and general condition and may order that the rent not exceed a specified amount. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf) The documents do not expressly say that a tenant may use this process simply to obtain a lower rent for pre-existing defects.

**Practical options under this version:** promptly document the defects with photographs and written descriptions; notify the landlord in writing; and, if you have not entered possession, consider giving a section 226 termination notice rather than moving in. Do not describe the keys issue as settled by the retrieved documents: they do not determine whether collecting keys alone means you entered possession.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) s 226 lets a renter who has not entered possession end the tenancy where the premises are "not in good repair" or "unfit for human habitation". (2) The landlord "must maintain the premises in good repair", the renter can request repairs in writing, and a condition making the premises "unsafe or insecure" counts as urgent repairs. (3) The hardest point is met through the evidence alternative: "promptly document the defects with photographs and written descriptions".

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the home must meet the rental minimum standards or a mould and damp standard; it relies on the 2019 Act's 'good repair' and 'unfit for human habitation' duties, and it does not say the renter must move in and pay rent, instead stating 'You may give the landlord a notice terminating the tenancy' under section 226 if they have not entered into possession.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
## What the law says

On **8 November 2022**, the applicable law was the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101** (in force from 7 September 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), and the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).

- Your rent must be paid at the place and in the manner specified in the lease, unless you and the rental provider agree to change the payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- If the agency is no longer acting, the owner must give you written notice of the change in the rental-provider/agent information. The notice must include the owner’s full name and address for service, and an emergency telephone number for urgent repairs; a change to this information must be notified within **7 days**. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)
- The prescribed lease form records the rental provider’s and agent’s details and says the rental provider must notify the renter within **7 days** if that information changes. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- The rental provider must provide a **fee-free payment method**, apart from fees charged by your own bank, and must permit Centrepay or another prescribed payment method. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)
- The bond is separate from rent: the rental provider or agent must lodge it with the RTBA within **10 business days** after receiving it. The RTBA must send you a receipt, and if you have not received one within **15 business days**, you may contact the RTBA. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

## What you can do or ask before paying

1. **Check the lease first:** confirm the rent amount, due date, payment method and payment details recorded in it. A new bank account does not itself change the agreed payment method; ask for written confirmation of the change. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

2. **Ask for the owner’s identifying and contact details:** request the owner’s full name and address for service, confirmation that the agency has stopped acting, and the emergency-repairs telephone number. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

3. **Verify the new account before transferring money:** ask the owner or agency to confirm, in writing, that the account is theirs and that it is for rent for your particular premises. The retrieved documents do not prescribe a separate bank-account verification procedure, so they do not say exactly how that verification must be done.

4. **Check your bond status:** make sure you received the RTBA bond receipt. If not, count **15 business days** from when you paid the bond and then contact the RTBA using the details in the prescribed form: **rtba@justice.vic.gov.au** or **1300 137 164**. [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)

5. **Keep evidence:** retain the lease, the agent’s change-of-details message, your request for confirmation, and any payment confirmation. You may request a rent receipt; for a payment not made in person, it must be provided within **5 business days** if requested when you make the payment. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer states the owner must give written notice of their 'full name and address for service, and an emergency telephone number for urgent repairs', with changes notified 'within 7 days'. (2) It states the bond must be lodged with the RTBA and tells the renter to check for the RTBA receipt. (3) The hardest point is covered by 'rent must be paid at the place and in the manner specified in the lease, unless you and the rental provider agree to change the payment method' together with 'ask the owner or agency to confirm, in writing, that the account is theirs… before transferring money'. The answer does not explicitly say to use a known contact, but confirming with the owner or agency is a reasonable next step consistent with the law.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter may withhold rent, and it requires written notice rather than permitting an unannounced change: 'the owner must give you written notice of the change' and 'ask for written confirmation of the change.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version 101 (in force from 7 September 2022)', linked as 97-109aa101, and relies only on that version and on the in-force 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, Authorised Version 002' (21-3sra002), with no rule taken from any other version.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 (Authorised Version v005)** and the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Authorised Version v111)**, both of which were in force on 3 December 2025, here is what the retrieved documents state regarding your situation:

### What the law says
**1. Do you have to be there yourself?**
The regulations state that a rental provider may enter the premises `"to do an inspection"` and that `"the renter must allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure"` [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). However, the retrieved excerpts **do not explicitly state** whether you are legally required to be physically present yourself to let the inspector in. They only establish that you must allow entry if the provider follows the correct legal procedure for access [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**2. Can they charge you a $90 rebooking fee?**
The retrieved documents **do not contain specific rules** about agents charging fees for rebooking inspections. However, they do state that any additional terms added to a rental agreement `"must not exclude, restrict or modify any of the rights and duties included in the Act"` and must comply with Australian Consumer Law (Victoria) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents explicitly note that unfair contract terms `"will have no effect"` [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

**3. Smoke alarm obligations**
Under the law, a residential rental provider has a strict duty to ensure that any smoke alarm installed in the rented premises is `"(a) correctly installed and in working condition; (b) fitted with batteries or replacement batteries; and (c) tested at least once every 12 months"` [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If a smoke alarm does not meet these requirements, you have the right to issue a request for urgent repairs [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

### What you can do or ask
*   **Ask for proof of proper procedure:** Request written confirmation from your agent detailing exactly how they followed the legal notice and access requirements for entering the premises for an inspection [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   **Question the fee:** Ask your agent to provide the specific clause in your tenancy agreement that permits a $90 rebooking fee, and request that they verify it complies with Australian Consumer Law, as unfair terms are legally void [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
*   **Verify the smoke alarm duty:** Remind your agent that testing smoke alarms is a mandatory legal duty for the rental provider to be completed at least once every 12 months, and you have the right to request urgent repairs if they fail to maintain them properly [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 088, which was in force on 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), here are your options regarding the damp, mould, and rotting timber you found before moving in:

### 🔑 Can you cancel or refuse to move in?
The Act does not use the word "cancel" for this scenario, but it gives you a clear right to refuse entry. Under section 65(1), your landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition on the agreed occupation day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the property has damp, mould, or rotting timber, it likely fails this standard. 

Section 65(2) explicitly states that you are **not required to enter into occupation** of premises that do not comply with this duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Furthermore, if you choose not to move in, section 65(3) protects you from paying rent for the period between the agreed start date and the day you actually enter (if you eventually do) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 🛠️ Can you ask for repairs?
Yes. Section 68(1) places a strict duty on your landlord to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You should formally notify your landlord or agent of the defects in writing. Depending on the severity, you have two main pathways:
* **Urgent Repairs:** If the damp/mould poses an immediate health or safety risk (e.g., structural rotting timber), it may qualify as an urgent repair. You can apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the landlord to fix it, and the Tribunal must hear your application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* **Non-Urgent Repairs:** If it is not immediately dangerous, you can apply to the Director of Housing to investigate whether the landlord is breaching their repair duty. If the issue remains unresolved after 14 days from your notice, and the Director's report doesn't satisfy you, you can then apply to the Tribunal for an order requiring the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 💰 Can you ask for lower rent?
The Act does not allow tenants to unilaterally reduce their rent. However, if the landlord fails to carry out required repairs after you have given proper notice, section 77 allows you to apply to the Tribunal for an order to pay your rent into a **Rent Special Account** (escrow) instead of paying the landlord directly [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal will only authorise this if satisfied that a repair notice has been given and the landlord has failed to comply with their duty [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 📝 Recommended Next Steps
1. Document the damp, mould, and rotting timber with photos/videos immediately.
2. Send a written notice to your landlord/agent citing section 65(1) (condition on occupation day) and section 68(1) (duty to maintain in good repair), stating you will not take possession until the issues are resolved.
3. If they refuse or delay, contact the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) or Consumer Affairs Victoria for guidance on filing an application under sections 73–75 or 77 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the home must meet rental minimum standards or a mould and damp standard. It relies only on the 2019 duties in s65 and s68, and it says the renter has a choice, quoting that the renter is "not required to enter into occupation" and is protected "from paying rent" until they enter.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:

### What the Law Says
* **Change of Management Details:** When an agent stops managing a property and the owner takes over, the owner must provide you with written notice of their full name, address for service of documents, and an emergency telephone number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
Based on the Victorian residential tenancy legislation in force on 3 December 2025, here is how your situation is covered:

### What the law says
* **Smoke alarm testing is the landlord's legal duty:** The residential rental provider must ensure that any smoke alarm installed in the rented premises is correctly installed, working, fitted with batteries, and tested at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). 
* **Entry rules:** The rental provider may enter your home to comply with their statutory duties (such as testing smoke alarms) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Your legal obligation is simply to `"allow entry to the premises where the rental provider has followed proper procedure"` [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The legislation does not explicitly state that *you personally* must be present, only that access must be provided.
* **Charging fees for inspections:** The standard residential tenancy agreement explicitly states that any additional terms `"must not exclude, restrict or modify any of the rights and duties included in the Act"` [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). There is no provision in the retrieved legislation that authorizes a rental provider to charge a tenant a fee for scheduling, rebooking, or attending a routine smoke alarm inspection.

### What you can do or ask
1. **Regarding being home:** Since your obligation is to `"allow entry"` rather than personally be present, you should ask your agent if you can arrange for another adult (e.g., a family member or neighbor) to let the inspector in, or if they hold a master key that permits them to enter after giving proper notice.
2. **Regarding the $90 fee:** You do not have to pay this fee. Because testing smoke alarms is a statutory duty of the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf), the administrative and operational costs of arranging these checks fall on the rental provider. A demand for a rebooking fee attempts to shift a landlord's legal cost onto you and would likely be considered an unauthorized term that restricts your rights under the Act [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You can politely decline the fee and request they proceed with their legal obligation to test the alarms at no cost to you.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Version 111** (which was in force on January 15, 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### Can the app charge you a card fee?
**Yes, provided a fee-free alternative is available and you are properly informed.** 
Under section 42(4) of the Act, your rental provider or their agent **must ensure that a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs (other than bank fees or account fees payable on your own bank account) is reasonably available to you** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Because your app offers a manual bank transfer option with no fee, this legal requirement is satisfied. 

While the law mandates a free option, it does not strictly prohibit third-party payment processors from charging their own credit/debit card processing fees. However, under section 42(7), the provider or agent **must give you information about any costs—including third party transaction fees—before you consent to use that payment method** [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

### Does it matter who receives the fee (the app company vs. the agent)?
**No, it does not change your legal rights.** 
The legislation places the obligation on the *rental provider or their agent* to provide a fee-free option and disclose any costs, regardless of who ultimately pockets the surcharge [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 
* If the **agent** charges the fee directly, they are imposing a cost that must be disclosed upfront.
* If the **app company** charges the fee, it is still classified as a "third party transaction fee" under the Act and must be clearly communicated to you before you agree to pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 

### What you can do or ask:
1. **Use the free option:** You are fully within your rights to use the manual bank transfer option with no fees, as the provider is legally required to keep it reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). 
2. **Check for disclosure:** If you haven't been explicitly told about the card fee *before* you agreed to use it, ask your agent/provider for proof that they disclosed these "third party transaction fees" as required by law [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
3. **Review the agreement:** The standard tenancy agreement notes that the provider must permit a fee-free method and allow electronic funds transfers or Centrepay [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), Authorised Version v088**, which was in force on 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf), here is how the law applies to your situation:

### 🔑 Can I cancel?
The provided text does not explicitly grant a statutory right to "cancel" a lease before possession. However, you have a strong legal right to **refuse to move in** until the issues are fixed. 
* Under section 65(1), a landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and in a reasonably clean condition on the agreed occupation day [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Damp, mould, and rotting timber likely breach this standard.
* Under section 65(2), you are **not required to enter into occupation** if the premises do not comply with that requirement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). 
* If you refuse to move in, section 65(3) states you **do not have to pay rent** for the period from the agreed occupation day until the day you actually enter [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 🛠️ Can I ask for repairs?
Yes. The landlord has a clear legal duty to fix these issues.
* Section 68(1) requires the landlord to ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Damp, mould, and rotting timber fall squarely under this maintenance obligation.
* You should give the landlord **written notice** specifying that these non-urgent repairs are required [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* If the landlord does not carry out the repairs within **14 days** of receiving your notice, you can apply to the Director to investigate the breach (section 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Following the Director's report, you can then apply to VCAT for a formal order requiring the landlord to carry out the specified repairs (section 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

### 💰 Can I ask for lower rent?
The Act does not provide a mechanism to simply "ask" a landlord for a voluntary rent reduction. However, it provides two financial protections relevant to your situation:
1. **Rent suspension until entry:** If you refuse to move in due to the poor condition, you legally owe $0 rent from the agreed start date until you actually take possession [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Rent Special Account:** If you do move in and give notice for repairs that the landlord then ignores, you can apply to VCAT under section 77 for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a Rent Special Account instead of directly to the landlord [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This holds the funds until the repair obligations are met or the matter is resolved.

### 📝 Immediate Steps You Should Take
* **Do not sign off on a clean condition report.** Section 35 requires the landlord to give you two copies of a condition report before you enter occupation, and you have 3 business days after entering to return one with endorsements [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Since you haven't moved in yet, explicitly note the damp, mould, and rotting timber on the report before signing it.
* **Document everything.** Take dated photos/videos of the defects and keep copies of all written communication with the landlord/agent regarding these issues.

*Note: This answer is based strictly on the provided excerpts from the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic) v088 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). For complex disputes or if the landlord refuses to address the condition, contacting VCAT or a community legal centre for tailored advice is recommended.*

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, Authorised Version No. 101 (in force on 8 November 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), here is what you should check and verify before paying rent into the new account:

### 1. Written Notice of New Contact Details
Because the owner is now managing the property themselves (meaning there is no longer an agent acting for them), they are legally required to provide you with written notice containing:
*   Their full name and address for the service of documents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
*   An emergency telephone number for urgent repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

The owner must give you this written notice before the end of the day after the change takes effect [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Do not pay into a new account until you have received this formal notification.

### 2. Agreement to Change Payment Method
Your rent is payable in the manner specified in your residential rental agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Paying into a completely different bank account constitutes a change to how rent is payable. 
*   You should ensure that **both you and the owner formally agree** to this change in writing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 
*   Once agreed, the new bank details should ideally be added as an addendum or written variation to your lease agreement to protect your payment history.

### 3. Bond Lodgement Details
Even though the management has changed, your bond must remain lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) under the correct residential rental provider's name [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 
*   If the owner is taking over the rights and duties from the agency or a previous landlord, they are legally required to notify the RTBA of this assignment/transfer within 5 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
*   You have the right to receive a copy of this notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Check that your bond records accurately reflect the new owner's name.

### 4. Receipts for Future Payments
Once you start paying into the new account, ensure the owner complies with receipt requirements:
*   If you pay in person, they must give you a written receipt immediately [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
*   If you pay electronically or by mail and request a receipt at the time of payment, they must provide it within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). 
*   The receipt must state your name, the rented premises, the date, the period covered, the amount paid, and clearly state that the payment is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

**Summary of Action:** Do not transfer the money until you have received written confirmation of the owner's new contact details, a signed agreement to change the payment method, and verification that your bond records with the RTBA are being updated correctly.
