question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic)**, specifically Authorised Version No. 088, which was in force on 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**1. Can you cancel or refuse to move in?**
Yes. Under section 65(1), your landlord is legally required to ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the day you are supposed to move in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Section 65(2) explicitly states that you are not required to enter into occupation if the premises do not meet this standard [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If you choose not to move in, section 65(3) confirms you do not have to pay rent for the period between the agreed start date and the day you actually enter (if you eventually do) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Can you ask for repairs?**
Yes. Under section 68(1), a landlord must ensure the rented premises are maintained in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). If the damp, mould, and rotting timber mean the premises are not in good repair, you can take these steps under Division 6 of the Act:
* Give the landlord written notice that repairs are required (section 74(1)(a)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* If the landlord does not carry out the repairs within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate whether the landlord is in breach of their duty (section 74(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* After receiving the Director's report, if satisfactory arrangements still haven't been made, you can apply to VCAT for an order requiring the landlord to carry out the specified repairs (section 75(1)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Can you ask for lower rent?**
The Act does not give tenants a direct right to unilaterally demand a lower rent. However, it provides a mechanism for rent relief if the landlord neglects necessary repairs:
* If you have given notice requiring repairs and the landlord fails to comply with their duty, you can apply to VCAT for an order authorising you to pay your rent into a "Rent Special Account" instead of directly to the landlord (section 77(1) and (2)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
* The Tribunal will decide how much rent is held in this account and may later order that some or all of it be paid to the landlord if they fulfill their repair duties (section 77(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

*(Note: If a declaration under the Housing Act 1983 declares the house unfit for habitation, the landlord is automatically in breach of section 68, though specific rights under sections 72–75 do not apply to breaches resulting from such a declaration) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).*

must-mention.reason: No. The answer never mentions the s 226 right of a renter who has not moved in to end the agreement by notice because the premises are not in good repair or are unfit. It bases cancellation on s 65 ('vacant and reasonably clean') rather than on disrepair or unfitness. It also does not say that serious damage making the home unsafe can be an urgent repair.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never claims the home must meet rental minimum standards or a mould and damp standard; it relies on the 2019-era duties (s65 'vacant and reasonably clean', s68 'maintained in good repair'), and it rejects any obligation to move in, stating 'you are not required to enter into occupation if the premises do not meet this standard' and 'you do not have to pay rent for the period between the agreed start date and the day you actually enter.'

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic), specifically Authorised Version No. 088' (link 97-109aa088), and every rule it applies (ss 65, 68, 74, 75, 77) is sourced from that version, which was in force on 15 October 2019.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
Based on the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997** (Vic), which was in force on 8 November 2022 (Authorised Version No. 101, effective from 7 September 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf), here is what the law requires and what you should verify before making your payment:

### What the Law Says
* **Notice of Change:** The residential rental provider must give you written notice of any change in their details (such as name, address for service, or phone number) before the end of [the relevant period] . 
* **Where and How Rent is Paid:** Rent is payable at the place specified in your lease agreement, or at the rented premises if no place is specified. It must also be paid in the manner (e.g., bank account details) specified in the agreement unless you and the provider agree to change it .
* **Payment Costs:** The provider or their agent must give you information about any costs (like transaction fees) associated with a payment method *before* you consent to use it .
* **Receipts:** Anyone who receives your rent must provide a written receipt. If paid in person, it must be given immediately. If not paid in person and you request a receipt at the time of payment, it must be provided within 5 business days .
* **Bond & Rights Transfer:** If the owner is taking over the rights and duties under the agreement from the agency, they must notify the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) within 5 days and give you a copy of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

### What You Should Check Before Paying
1. **Written Notice of the New Details:** Ask for formal written confirmation that the agent's authority has ended and that the owner is now managing the property. This notice must include the owner's full name, address for service of documents, and an emergency telephone number .
2. **Lease Agreement Terms:** Check your signed lease to see if it specifies a particular bank account or payment method. The owner cannot unilaterally change this without your agreement .
3. **Associated Fees:** Ask the owner to confirm in writing that there are no additional transaction fees, direct debit dishonour fees, or other costs you will incur by using their new bank details before you agree to use them .
4. **Bond Lodgment Status:** Verify that your bond is correctly lodged with the RTBA under the owner's name (or confirm the transfer notice has been provided) so your security deposit remains protected [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Request a Receipt:** When you make the payment into the new account, explicitly request a written receipt to protect yourself and ensure the payment is properly recorded .

must-mention.reason: No. The 7-day deadline in point 1 (s 66) is missing: the answer says notice of a change in details must be given 'before the end of [the relevant period]', an unfilled placeholder, so the reader is never told the period is 7 days. Point 3 is also weak, because the answer never advises confirming the new bank details with the agency or landlord through a known contact before paying.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never suggests withholding rent and instead says the provider 'must give you written notice of any change in their details' and that 'The owner cannot unilaterally change this without your agreement', so neither failure condition is asserted.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (Vic) ... Authorised Version No. 101, effective from 7 September 2022' and links to 97-109aa101, which is the version in force on 8 November 2022, and it relies on no other version.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Document used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf", Authorised Version No. 111. It is dated 25 November 2025 and in force until 29 June 2026, so it was the version in force on 3 December 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I also looked at the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf", dated 25 November 2025 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The text I retrieved doesn't print an Authorised Version number for the Regulations. The file metadata lists "version 005".

## What the law says

**Smoke alarm checks are the rental provider's duty.** The provider must make sure smoke alarms work and are tested at least once every 12 months. Testing or repair of a mains-powered alarm must be done by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Entry for the check.**
- The provider or agent may enter at a time agreed with you, if you consented within the 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Otherwise they may enter between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday. For entry to carry out a duty under the Act, they must give at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must be in writing and say why they want to enter. It must be given by post, or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- They must enter in a reasonable manner and not stay longer than necessary without your consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- You have a duty to permit entry that follows these rules [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

## Do you have to be home?

The retrieved sections don't say you must be present. They also don't say you may be absent. They only say you must permit entry if it follows the rules above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The 10 am–12:30 pm weekday window falls within the 8 a.m.–6 p.m. range, as long as a valid written notice was given with at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say what happens if no one is home.

## Can they charge $90?

The documents I retrieved don't answer this. Section 51 ("Certain charges prohibited") appears in the table of contents [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf), but its text wasn't in what I retrieved. The only fee provision I saw is section 84, which concerns fees for consenting to assignment or sub-letting and isn't relevant here [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). So I can't say whether the $90 rebooking fee is allowed.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for the written notice.** Check that it states the reason, was given by post or by hand during 8 a.m.–6 p.m., and gave at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Propose a time that suits you.** Entry can be at any time you agree to, if you consent within 7 days before it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent which section of the Act allows the $90 fee.** I couldn't confirm one in the retrieved text.
- **Apply to the Tribunal if needed.** You can apply for an order limiting when entry may occur [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If the agent enters without following the rules, you can apply to restrain further entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entering outside the rules without reasonable excuse carries a penalty of 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: No. The first point is missing because the answer is hedged both ways. It says "The retrieved sections don't say you must be present" but then adds "They also don't say you may be absent" and "The documents don't say what happens if no one is home." A reader cannot tell whether they need to be home, and the answer never says the agent can let the inspector in. The second point (the landlord's duty, 24 hours' written notice, 8 am to 6 pm) is covered.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must be home; it says "The retrieved sections don't say you must be present". It never says the fee must be paid; it says "I can't say whether the $90 rebooking fee is allowed."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as 'Authorised Version No. 111' (file rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf, link 97-109aa111) and the Regulations as 'version 005' (file rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf, link 21-3sra005, dated 25 November 2025), and every rule it applies is cited to the in-force Act version 111.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
**Short answer:** The documents don't give a clear yes or no on whether the card fee is lawful. Section 51(3) probably covers it, but I'm interpreting that. Because you have a free option, the agent's main obligation under s 42(4) looks met.

**Documents used (in force on 15 Jan 2026)**
- *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file `rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf`, dated 25 Nov 2025, version 111. It was in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The retrieved text doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No.", so I'm using the file's version label.
- *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file `rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf`, dated 25 Nov 2025, version 005. It was in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **A free method must be available.** The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs (other than your own bank fees) is reasonably available to you (s 42(4)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Your bank transfer fits this. The documents don't say that a slower method fails the "reasonably available" test.
- **You must be told about costs first.** Before you consent to a payment method, the provider or agent must tell you about any costs, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees (s 42(7)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Electronic payment facility charges are restricted.** A person must not demand or receive a charge for the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or "any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units (s 51(3)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A card fee may fall within this, but the documents don't define "electronic payment facility" or mention card surcharges specifically. I can't confirm it is covered.
- **Payment method rules.** Electronic funds transfer is a prescribed method the agent must permit [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). A term requiring rent in advance by a payment method with extra costs is a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## Does it matter whether the app or the agent gets the fee?

- **Section 51(3):** Probably not. It applies to "a person", so it isn't limited to the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Sections 42(4) and 42(7):** These bind only the provider and the agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51A:** This bans businesses other than the provider, the agent and banks from charging prescribed rent-payment fees. It would aim at a third-party app company [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). But the regulation listing the prescribed matters, including "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)", only has effect on and after 31 March 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). On 15 January 2026 the documents don't show it operating. The documents don't say which surcharges "any other Act" permits.

## What you can do

- Pay by bank transfer and avoid the fee.
- Ask the agent in writing for the cost information that s 42(7) requires before you consent to card payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Ask the agent to agree a different, faster fee-free method. The Act allows the provider and renter to change how rent is paid by agreement (s 42(6)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- If you've already been charged, you could raise s 51(3) with the agent, but whether it applies to a card fee isn't settled in these documents.

The documents don't say where to complain or how to get a fee refunded.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered: the answer says a method with no additional costs (other than the renter's own bank fees) must be reasonably available and that 'Your bank transfer fits this'. For the hardest point it says the regulation listing the prescribed fees 'only has effect on and after 31 March 2026. On 15 January 2026 the documents don't show it operating.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer says neither failing claim, stating that the s 51A prescribed-matters regulation 'only has effect on and after 31 March 2026' and that 'On 15 January 2026 the documents don't show it operating', and affirming that 'The provider or agent must ensure a rent payment method with no additional costs ... is reasonably available to you (s 42(4))'.

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 111" (file `rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf`, link 97-109aa111) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as "version 005" (file `rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf`, link 21-3sra005), both dated 25 Nov 2025 and in force on 15 January 2026; it relies on no other version and notes only that the prescribed-matters regulation in version 005 takes effect on 31 March 2026.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Document applied:** *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). It is dated 2 July 2019, and its metadata shows it in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). That covers 15 October 2019.

The Act's main text in this version still uses "tenant" and "landlord". Its endnotes list the Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2018 changes (renaming to "renter" and "residential rental provider", and new rental minimum standards) among provisions "Not in Operation" at the date of publication [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I have therefore relied on the main text and not on those later changes.

## What the law says

- **Landlord's duty:** The landlord must keep the premises "in good repair" (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Cancelling before you move in:** A tenancy agreement terminates if you have not entered into possession and you give the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises:
  - (a) "are not in good repair"
  - (b) "are unfit for human habitation"
  - (c) are destroyed or unsafe
  - (d) are not vacant
  - (e) are not legally available for use as a residence
  - (f) are "for any other reason unavailable for occupation" (s 226) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf)
- **Vacant and clean on the agreed day:** The landlord must ensure the premises are vacant and reasonably clean on the agreed move-in day. You are not required to move in if they aren't, and you don't pay rent from the agreed day until you actually move in (s 65) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This section covers vacancy and cleanliness. The retrieved text does not say that damp or rot falls under it.

## Your options

**1. Cancel (s 226).** Because you haven't moved in, you can give the landlord a notice of termination on the "not in good repair" ground. The "unfit for human habitation" or "unavailable for occupation" grounds may also fit [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Whether damp, mould and rotting timber meet any of these grounds depends on the facts, and the Act text doesn't settle that. The documents don't set out a required form or notice period for this notice. Don't move in before you give notice, because s 226 only applies if you haven't "entered into possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**2. Ask for repairs.**
- **Non-urgent repairs:** Give the landlord written notice. If the repairs aren't done within 14 days, you can apply to the Director to investigate (s 74) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - After the Director's report, you can apply to the Tribunal within 60 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - If you haven't received the report within 90 days, you can apply to the Tribunal without it (s 75) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The Tribunal can order specified repairs and set a deadline (s 76) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Urgent repairs:** The list in this version includes a "serious roof leak" and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Mould and damp are named as urgent only in the 2018 amendments, which are listed as not in operation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - If your problem does count as urgent, you may arrange the repairs yourself, but only after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord to do them and being unable to. You must give 14 days' written notice, and the landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less (s 72) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You can also apply to the Tribunal for urgent repairs, and it must hear the application within 2 business days (s 73) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account:** Once you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal for an order to pay rent into the Rent Special Account (s 77) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The Tribunal can make the order if the landlord has failed to do the repairs. This holds the rent but doesn't reduce it.

**3. Lower rent.** The retrieved text gives no direct right to cut the rent yourself for defects at the start of a tenancy.
- You may complain to the Director about excessive rent only where the landlord has reduced or withdrawn services or facilities, or after a rent-increase notice (s 45) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- If the Tribunal then considers the rent, it must take into account "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" (s 47(3)(b)) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The only rent relief for the period before you move in is under s 65(3), and it applies to premises that aren't vacant or reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- I found nothing in the retrieved text on how a rent reduction for damp or mould would work.

## Practical steps
- Record the defects in writing and with photos.
- If you move in, the landlord must give you a condition report before you enter. You must return a signed copy, or one noting any disagreement, within 3 business days of moving in (s 35) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- A condition report signed by both parties is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition, except for defects that couldn't reasonably have been found on inspection, or parts you have disagreed with in writing (s 36) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover compensation for cancelling, or what happens to your bond or any rent already paid. I can't say more on those from these sources.

All three points are covered: s 226 lets a renter who hasn't moved in end the agreement on the 'not in good repair' or 'unfit for human habitation' grounds; s 68 and the repair and urgent-repair options, including 'any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure', are stated; and the hardest point, that cancelling depends on disrepair or unfitness rather than mere uncleanliness, is covered by the answer separating s 65 ('This section covers vacancy and cleanliness') from the s 226 grounds and advising 'Record the defects in writing and with photos.'

It does not say the renter must move in and pay rent; it offers cancellation instead ('you can give the landlord a notice of termination on the "not in good repair" ground').

This is the version in force on 15 October 2019, and the answer applies only its rules. question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Documents used:** the *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf" (version 101, dated 7 Sept 2022, in force until 23 May 2023), and the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf" (version 002, dated 1 June 2022). Both were in force on 8 November 2022. The retrieved text doesn't print the words "Authorised Version No.", so I'm giving the version numbers from the file names and metadata.

## What the law says

- **The rent details are set by the agreement.** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, and in the manner specified in it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The rental provider and renter can change the manner of payment by agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Act doesn't say the provider can change it alone, so a new bank account is something to confirm and agree.
- **A change in who manages the property must be notified in writing.**
  - If an agent acts, the provider must give the renter the agent's name, address for service and phone number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - If no agent acts, the provider must give their own full name, address for service and an emergency phone number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - Any change in this information must be notified in writing within 7 days after the change [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - The standard lease form says the same [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Payment options.**
  - The provider or agent must ensure a payment method with no extra cost, other than your own bank fees, is reasonably available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - They must allow Centrepay and the prescribed method, which is electronic funds transfer [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
  - They must tell you about any transaction or other fees before you consent to a payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts.**
  - If you pay by transfer and ask for a receipt when you pay, the receiver must give a written receipt within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - The receipt must be signed. It must state your name and the premises, the date received, the period covered, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
  - If no receipt is required, the receiver must keep a record of the payment for 12 months. If you ask for a copy, they must give it within 5 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can check and ask

1. **Get the change in writing from the owner.** Ask for their full name, address for service and emergency number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Ask for the new bank details in writing too. Check your lease's payment-details section, which is where the lease form records them [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
2. **Agree the change in writing.** Reply that you agree to the new payment manner once the above is confirmed [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Confirm the new account independently.** Contact the owner using details you already hold, such as those in your lease. Do the same with the agency. The documents I retrieved don't set out any verification procedure, so this is practical caution and not a legal requirement.
4. **Ask about fees.** Confirm the new method is free apart from your own bank fees, and ask what costs apply [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask for a receipt when you pay.** Make the request at the time of payment so the 5-business-day deadline applies [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Check the bond.**
   - Your bond should be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - If you haven't had the Authority's receipt within 15 business days of paying, you can notify the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
   - If the provider is actually assigning or transferring their rights and duties to someone else, they must notify the Authority within 5 days. They must also give you a copy of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

The documents don't say whether the agency's message alone is enough to change the payment details. They also don't say what happens if you pay into an account that turns out to be wrong.

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered: the answer says that if no agent acts the provider must give their 'full name, address for service and an emergency phone number' and that 'any change in this information must be notified in writing within 7 days'; it says the bond 'should be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority' and that the renter can notify the Authority if no receipt arrives; and it says the parties 'can change the manner of payment by agreement' and advises contacting 'the owner using details you already hold... Do the same with the agency.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never suggests withholding rent, and it rejects unilateral changes by stating 'Any change in this information must be notified in writing within 7 days after the change' and 'The Act doesn't say the provider can change it alone, so a new bank account is something to confirm and agree.'

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as "version 101, dated 7 Sept 2022" (file rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf, link 97-109aa101), which is the version in force on 8 November 2022, and it relies on no other version except the in-force Regulations "version 002, dated 1 June 2022" (21-3sra002).

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
## What the law says

I used the **Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111** (incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026, so it applies on 3 December 2025. I also used the **Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021** (file `rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf`, version 005, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The regulations text I retrieved doesn't show an "Authorised Version No." label, so that version number comes from the file metadata.

**Do you have to be home?**
- A rental provider must test smoke alarms at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Mains-powered alarms must be tested by a suitably qualified person [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- An agent may enter between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday. For entry to carry out the provider's duty under the Act, that needs at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm check fits this ground, though that is my inference. The documents don't name smoke alarm checks as an entry purpose.
- The notice must be in writing, say why they want to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Alternatively, they can enter at a time you agreed, if you consented within the 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- You have a duty to *permit* entry that is made in accordance with these rules [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents I retrieved do not say you must be present. They only require that you not obstruct a lawful entry. I can't say from them whether the agent can insist you stay home.
- Entry must be in a reasonable manner, and they can't stay longer than necessary without your consent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Can they charge $90?**
- The documents contain no provision allowing a "rebooking fee" for a smoke alarm check.
- A person must not demand or accept from a renter who has failed to comply with the agreement or Act any amount other than rent or an amount provided for in the Act. The penalty is 150 penalty units for a natural person and 750 for a body corporate [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- A lease term that imposes fees for safety-related maintenance that is the rental provider's responsibility is a prescribed prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). A prohibited term is void and unenforceable [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Smoke alarm testing is the provider's duty, so this probably covers the fee. That is my reading, and the regulations don't mention smoke alarms in that provision.
- I can't tell from the documents whether your lease contains this fee.

## What you can do

- **Ask for the written notice.** Check that it gives at least 24 hours' notice, states the reason, and falls between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Propose a time.** The Act lets you and the agent agree a time, as long as you consent within 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent which section or lease term authorises the $90 fee.** I found none. Refuse to pay it, and refer to the provisions above [[3]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- **Apply to the Tribunal.** You can apply for an order limiting the days and times of entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). If an agent exercises entry without following the rules, you can apply for an order restraining entry for a set period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Report improper entry.** An agent who enters other than in accordance with these rules, without reasonable excuse, commits an offence carrying 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

I'd avoid blocking a properly notified entry. Failing to permit it can be treated as a breach of your duty under the Act [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both required points are covered, though the second depends on reading the rubric's seven-day clause leniently. Point 1: the answer says "The documents I retrieved do not say you must be present. They only require that you not obstruct a lawful entry." The rubric explicitly accepts both 'documents do not say' and 'need only not obstruct' wording. Point 2: it says smoke alarm testing is the rental provider's duty, and that entry to carry out a duty needs at least 24 hours' written notice, stating the reason, between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. It does not state that 'seven days given' satisfies the notice requirement. However, the user's question never mentions seven days of notice, so that clause cannot reasonably count against the answer, and the substance of the point is present.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter must be home or must pay the fee: it states "The documents I retrieved do not say you must be present," and on the fee it says "I found none. Refuse to pay it."

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111' (link 97-109aa111) and the 'Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021' as 'version 005' (file rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf, link 21-3sra005). Every cited source, including [3], points to these in-force versions, and no rule comes from any other version.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says

**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, file "rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf" (dated 25 Nov 2025, version 111, in force 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021*, file "rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf" (dated 25 Nov 2025, version 005, in force to 9 Feb 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 15 January 2026. I'm taking the version numbers from the documents' metadata. The retrieved text doesn't show an "Authorised Version" label.

**1. A fee-free option must be reasonably available (s 42(4)).**
- The rental provider or their agent must ensure a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs, other than fees on your own bank account, is reasonably available to you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The standard-form agreement repeats this. The provider must permit a fee-free payment method other than the renter's own bank fees [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
- Your free bank transfer therefore appears to meet this duty. The documents don't define "reasonably available", so they don't say whether "slower" changes that.

**2. Fees must be disclosed first (s 42(7)).**
- The provider or agent must tell you about any costs you may incur by using a payment method before you consent to it. This expressly includes third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- That wording shows the Act contemplates that some payment methods carry fees.

**3. Some charges are banned outright (s 51(3)).**
- A person must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for the first issue of a rent payment card [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- A person must not demand or receive a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The documents don't say whether a card-payment surcharge counts as a charge for using an "electronic payment facility". I can't give you a definite yes or no on that.

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

It may, but the documents only partly answer this.

- **Fee to the agent or rental provider:** The s 42(4) duty applies to them, as does s 42(7) disclosure [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Section 51(3) applies to "a person", so it isn't limited to who receives the money [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Fee to a separate app company:**
  - Section 51A bars a business, other than the provider, the provider's agent or a bank-type deposit-taking institution, from demanding or receiving a fee for "any prescribed matter" relating to rent payment [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
  - The retrieved Regulations don't list any prescribed matter for s 51A [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). I can't say whether a card fee is covered.
  - Section 51A is marked as inserted by Act No. 6/2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't give a start date for it.

## What you can do

- **Use the free bank transfer.** The fee-free option is what the Act requires to be available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask in writing for details of the fee.** This should cover the amount, who receives it, and who runs the payment facility. The agent must disclose costs before you consent to a method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent to confirm the fee-free method.** If it isn't reasonably available, s 42(4) may be breached [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Check your agreement.** A term requiring rent in advance by a method with extra costs is a prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). You and the provider can also agree to change how rent is paid [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

The retrieved documents don't cover how to make a complaint or enforce these rules, so I can't advise on that.

must-mention.reason: No. The second point is missing: the answer never says the rent-payment fee ban (reg 21C) is not yet in effect on 15 January 2026, or that it starts on 31 March 2026, and instead says only that 'The retrieved Regulations don't list any prescribed matter for s 51A' and 'The documents don't give a start date for it.' The first point is covered by 'Your free bank transfer therefore appears to meet this duty.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer does not claim the card fee is already banned under s 51A or reg 21C, and it affirms a fee-free rule exists: it says the provider must ensure 'a rent payment method that incurs no additional costs... is reasonably available' under s 42(4), and on s 51A says 'The retrieved Regulations don't list any prescribed matter for s 51A... I can't say whether a card fee is covered.'

version-cited.reason: Yes: the answer names both required documents with their in-force versions, the Act as "version 111" (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf, link 97-109aa111) and the Regulations as "version 005" (rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf, link 21-3sra005), and every rule it applies comes from those versions.

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Document used:** *rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 088, which incorporates amendments as at 2 July 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it was in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- The landlord must keep the rented premises "in good repair" (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Two provisions do apply to premises that are not in a fit state before you move in:
  - If the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for human habitation, or are unavailable for occupation for any other reason, the tenancy ends if you have not yet entered into possession and you give the landlord a notice of termination on that ground (s 226) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - Section 226 lists those grounds as (a) not in good repair, (b) unfit for human habitation, and (f) unavailable for occupation for any other reason [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- Some newer amendments are not in operation in this version. They include adding "mould or damp" to urgent repairs, adding a "rental minimum standards" ground to the pre-possession termination provision, and the change from "tenant" to "renter" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The document lists the amending provisions as "Not in Operation" at its publication date [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). I have therefore relied on the main text only.

## Your options

**1. Cancel the lease before moving in**
- You can give the landlord a notice of termination under s 226, on the grounds that the premises are not in good repair, are unfit for habitation, or are unavailable for occupation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- This only works if you have "not entered into possession" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether collecting the keys counts as entering into possession. Don't move in or move belongings in until you've resolved this.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- *Urgent repairs:*
  - The definition includes a "serious roof leak" and "any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). Damp, mould and rotting timber aren't named in the in-force definition, so whether yours qualifies depends on how serious the fault is.
  - If it qualifies, you may arrange the repairs yourself, but only after taking reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them immediately and being unable to [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You must give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and their cost [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost or $1000, whichever is less [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You can also apply to VCAT for an order for urgent repairs, and the Tribunal must hear it within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- *Non-urgent repairs:*
  - Give the landlord written notice. If the repairs aren't done within 14 days, you can apply in writing to the Director to investigate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You can then apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving the Director's report. You can also apply if you haven't received the report within 90 days of asking for it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - If the Tribunal finds a breach of the duty to maintain, it may order specified repairs and must set a deadline [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- *Rent into the Rent Special Account:* once you've given notice requiring repairs, you can ask the Tribunal to let you pay rent into the Rent Special Account. The Tribunal may order this if the landlord has failed to do the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The documents give no automatic right to reduce rent yourself because of defects.
- A duty-breach route may lead to a rent reduction:
  - Section 68 is a "duty provision" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - You can give a breach of duty notice, which must specify the breach, the loss, and require the landlord to remedy or compensate within the required time. For these duties that is 14 days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - If the landlord doesn't comply, you can apply to the Tribunal for a compensation or compliance order [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The Tribunal can order the breach remedied, compensation paid, or the landlord to refrain from repeating it. Compensation may take the form of "a refund or reduction of the rent" [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The "excessive rent" complaint to the Director applies where the landlord has reduced services or where you've received a rent increase notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). It doesn't clearly fit your situation. If it did apply, the Tribunal considers "the state of repair and general condition" of the premises [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Practical point

Record the defects in the condition report. A signed condition report is conclusive evidence of the premises' condition, unless it was endorsed with your disagreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). You must return your copy within 3 business days after entering occupation, signed or endorsed as agreeing or disagreeing [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Not covered

The documents don't say whether collecting keys means you've "entered into possession". They don't set a notice period for a s 226 termination. They also don't say whether damp, mould and rotting timber is "unfit for human habitation" in your case.

must-mention.reason: Yes. The answer covers all three points: s 226 lets a tenant who has not entered possession terminate because the premises are 'not in good repair' or 'unfit for human habitation'; s 68 requires good repair, with repair routes including urgent repairs for 'any fault or damage that makes rented premises… unsafe or insecure'; and the hardest point is covered because cancellation is tied to disrepair or unfitness, the answer notes the documents don't say whether 'damp, mould and rotting timber is "unfit for human habitation" in your case', and it advises recording the defects in the condition report as evidence.

must-not-say.reason: Yes: the answer asserts neither failure condition. It says the 'rental minimum standards' ground and the 'mould or damp' urgent-repair addition are 'Not in Operation' in this version, and it presents cancellation under s 226 as an option rather than saying the renter must move in and pay rent.
