It mentions the not-yet-operative amendments (mould or damp in urgent repairs, rental minimum standards) only to say they do not apply, and it bases its rules on the version 088 main text.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
**Documents used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997* (file rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf, version 101, dated 7 September 2022, in force 7 Sept 2022 to 23 May 2023) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I also used the *Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021* (file rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf, version 002, dated 1 June 2022, in force 1 June 2022 to 30 Nov 2024) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Both were in force on 8 November 2022. The excerpts I retrieved show the version number only in the file metadata, not as a printed "Authorised Version No." line.

## What the law says

- **Where and how rent is paid:** Rent is payable at the place specified in the agreement, or at the premises if none is specified. It is payable in the manner specified in the agreement [1, s 42(1)–(2)]. The provider and renter may change the manner of payment *by agreement* [1, s 42(6)].
- **No-cost and electronic payment:** The provider or their agent must make a payment method with no extra cost (other than your own bank fees) reasonably available. They must also permit payment by Centrepay and any prescribed method [1, s 42(4)–(5)]. The prescribed method is electronic funds transfer [2, reg 19]. They must tell you about any fees before you consent to a payment method [1, s 42(7)].
- **Change of agent or provider details:** If there is no agent, the provider must give you their full name, an address for service of documents and an emergency phone number. If there is an agent, they must give the agent's details instead [1, s 66(2)–(3)]. The provider must tell you in writing of any change in that information within 7 days after the change [1, s 66(4)]. The standard agreement form also records the provider's and agent's details and notes the 7-day duty to notify changes [2, Form 1, item 3].
- **Receipts:** Anyone who receives rent must give a written receipt. If you pay by transfer and ask for a receipt when you pay, it is due within 5 business days. The receipt must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid for, the amount, and that it is for rent [1, s 43(1), (3)]. If no receipt is required, the recipient must keep a record for 12 months. If you ask for a copy, they must give it within 5 business days [1, s 43(2), (2A)].

## What you can check or ask

1. **Ask for the change in writing.** The Act requires written notice of a change in who is acting (owner instead of agent) [1, s 66(4)]. Ask for the owner's full name, address for service and emergency number [1, s 66(2)].
2. **Compare the details with your lease.** Check the "payment details" and provider/agent details in your agreement [2, Form 1, items 3 and 8]. A different bank account is a change in the manner of payment, which the Act says is done by agreement [1, s 42(6)]. You can ask for the change to be agreed in writing.
3. **Check there is no extra cost.** Confirm that a no-cost method, including electronic transfer, remains available [1, s 42(4)–(5); 2, reg 19], and ask about any fees [1, s 42(7)].
4. **Ask for receipts.** Request a receipt when you pay, so the owner has to issue one that meets the s 43(3) requirements [1, s 43(1), (3)].
5. **Check your bond receipt.** The standard form says the bond must be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority within 10 business days of payment, and the Authority sends you a receipt. If you have none within 15 business days of paying, you can email rtba@justice.vic.gov.au or call the Authority [2, Form 1, item 7]. The number printed there is 1300 137 164 in Form 1 and 1300 13 71 64 in Form 2, so check which is correct.

**Not covered:** The retrieved documents don't say whether an unverified change of bank account is valid, or how to verify that the new account belongs to the owner. They also don't say what happens if you pay into a wrong account. To confirm the change independently, use the contact details in your signed agreement, not only those in the new message.

**Timing:** These provisions apply to agreements made after the 2018 amendments. The Act has transitional rules for older tenancies [1, Sch 1, cl 16]. A recently signed lease should not be affected.

must-mention.reason: Yes, all three points are covered. (1) It states the s 66 duty to give the full name, address for service and emergency phone number, and to notify changes in writing within 7 days. (2) It states the bond must be lodged with the Residential Tenancies Bond Authority and tells the renter to check for the Authority's receipt, citing Form 1 rather than s 406–407 but with the same substance. (3) For the hardest point, it says a different bank account 'is a change in the manner of payment, which the Act says is done by agreement [s 42(6)]' and advises 'To confirm the change independently, use the contact details in your signed agreement, not only those in the new message.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter may withhold rent, and it requires notice and agreement for the change, stating that 'The provider must tell you in writing of any change in that information within 7 days after the change' and that 'A different bank account is a change in the manner of payment, which the Act says is done by agreement.'

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act with its version, quoting 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997 (file rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf, version 101, dated 7 September 2022...)' and its link 97-109aa101. The only other document it relies on is the Regulations at 'version 002, dated 1 June 2022' (link 21-3sra002), which was also in force on 8 November 2022, and no rule is taken from any other version.

question: Today is Wednesday 3 December 2025. My agent says I must be home for a smoke alarm check on a weekday between 10 am and 12:30 pm, or pay a $90 fee to rebook. Do I have to be there myself to let the inspector in, and can they charge me the $90?
answer:
**Documents used:** *rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf* is the Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111, incorporating amendments as at 25 November 2025 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Its metadata shows it in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 29 Jun 2026, so it was the version in force on 3 December 2025. I also checked *rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf*, the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021. Its metadata labels it version 005 and shows it in force from 25 Nov 2025 to 9 Feb 2026 [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

**Smoke alarm duty.** The rental provider must make sure any smoke alarm is correctly installed, working, fitted with batteries, and tested at least once every 12 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). This is s 68AA.

**Right of entry.**
- The provider or agent may enter at a time you've agreed to, if you consented within the 7 days before entry [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Otherwise they may enter between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. on any day except a public holiday, with notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- Entry to carry out a duty under the Act needs at least 24 hours' notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). A smoke alarm test seems to fall here, since it is a duty under s 68AA. That is my reading, not wording in the documents.
- A routine inspection needs at least 7 days' notice, and can't be done if one was made in the last 6 months [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- The notice must be in writing, say why they want to enter, and be given by post or delivered personally between 8 a.m. and 6 p.m. [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- They must enter in a reasonable manner and not stay longer than necessary [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Do you have to be home?** The retrieved provisions don't say so. You have a duty to *permit* entry that complies with the Division [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). That means you must not block a lawful entry. Nothing in the retrieved text requires you to be present to let the inspector in. The provisions also don't say how entry is physically carried out, such as with a key, so they don't answer that. A 10 am–12:30 pm window is within the 8 a.m.–6 p.m. hours, but the documents don't give a "weekday-only" rule [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**Can they charge $90?** The documents I retrieved don't answer this.
- Nothing in the retrieved provisions authorises a rebooking fee for a missed entry.
- The Act's contents list includes s 51, "Certain charges prohibited", and s 51A on certain application and rent payment fees [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The text of those sections wasn't retrieved, so I can't say whether they cover this fee.

## What you can do or ask

- **Ask for the notice in writing.** It should state the purpose and give at least 24 hours' notice, or 7 days if it's really a general inspection [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Offer an agreed time.** If you agree a time within 7 days of entry, they can enter then [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Ask the agent for the legal basis of the $90 fee.** The retrieved documents don't show one.
- **If they enter without following the rules,** you can apply to the Tribunal for an order restraining entry for a set period [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). Entering otherwise than in accordance with the Division, without reasonable excuse, is an offence with a penalty of 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **If you need to limit when entry happens,** you can apply to the Tribunal for an order specifying or limiting entry times [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Check s 51 yourself.** I'd confirm the fee question against the full text of s 51 of the Act. The standard agreement also lists the rental provider's safety duties, including smoke alarms [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

I haven't seen your agreement or the agent's notice, so I can't say whether this particular notice complies.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. Point 1: the answer says 'You have a duty to *permit* entry... That means you must not block a lawful entry. Nothing in the retrieved text requires you to be present.' Point 2: it identifies smoke alarm testing as the provider's s 68AA duty and states that entry for a duty needs at least 24 hours' written notice within 8 a.m.–6 p.m. It does not confirm that seven days' notice was given, but the user never mentioned a notice period, so it could not reasonably apply that fact.

must-not-say.reason: Yes, pass: the output asserts neither failure point. On presence it says "Nothing in the retrieved text requires you to be present to let the inspector in." On the fee it says "Nothing in the retrieved provisions authorises a rebooking fee for a missed entry," so it never claims the renter must be home or must pay the $90.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Act as 'Residential Tenancies Act 1997, Authorised Version No. 111' (link 97-109aa111) and the Regulations as 'rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf ... version 005' (link 21-3sra005), both versions in force on 3 December 2025, and every rule it applies comes only from these versions.

question: It's the middle of January 2026 (Thursday the 15th). My rent app charges a fee when I pay by card. There's also a manual bank transfer option with no fee, but it's slower. Can the app charge me the card fee? Does it matter whether the fee goes to the app company or to the agent?
answer:
## What the law says (as at 15 January 2026)

**Documents applied:**
- *rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 111, dated 25 Nov 2025, in force to 29 June 2026) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- *rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 005, dated 25 Nov 2025, in force to 9 Feb 2026) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The documents give version numbers, not the words "Authorised Version No." The version numbers above come from the file names and metadata.

**1. A free payment method must be reasonably available.** The rental provider or their agent must make sure a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you. Your own bank or account fees don't count as additional costs. The penalty is 80 penalty units for a natural person and 400 for a body corporate [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The standard rental agreement form repeats this: a fee-free method (other than your own bank fees) must be permitted [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf). The documents don't define "reasonably available", so I can't say whether "slower" makes a bank transfer unreasonable.

**2. You must be told about costs first.** The provider or agent must give you information about any costs, including third-party transaction fees and other electronic payment facility fees. They must do this before you consent to using that payment method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).

**3. There is a ban on charges for electronic payment facilities.** Under s 51(3)(b), "a person" must not demand or receive from a renter a charge for "the establishment or use of direct debit facilities or any other electronic payment facility for payment of rent". The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a card option in a rent app counts as an "electronic payment facility". If it does, this section could stop the card fee even though a free transfer exists. I can't confirm that from the documents.

## Does it matter who gets the fee?

- **Sections 42(4) and 42(7)** only bind the rental provider and their agent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51(3)** applies to "a person", so it isn't limited to the agent. It could cover an app company as well [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Section 51A** bans a business (other than a rental provider, their agent, or a bank) from charging a fee for a "prescribed matter" relating to rent payment. That is aimed at third parties like an app company. The penalty is 80 or 400 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
  - The regulation that prescribes "rent payment (other than payment surcharge fees permitted under any other Act)" only takes effect **on and after 31 March 2026** [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).
  - So on 15 January 2026, the documents don't show s 51A catching an app's card fee yet.
  - The documents don't say which "other Act" permits surcharges.

## What you can do

- **Ask in writing** which payment methods are fee-free, and for the full cost details of the card option, before you agree to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Stick with the free bank transfer.** Nothing in the documents lets an agent force you onto a fee-charging method. The rules require a fee-free option to be available [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Query the card fee itself** under s 51(3)(b), particularly if the agent receives the fee [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/97-109aa111-authorised.pdf).
- **Check the agreement.** A term requiring you to pay rent in advance by a method with extra costs is a prescribed prohibited term [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-11/21-3sra005-authorised.pdf).

The documents don't cover how to complain or enforce these rules, so I can't advise on that. They also don't include any version of the Regulations after 9 February 2026.

must-mention.reason: Yes. Both points are covered. The answer says a fee-free method (other than the renter's own bank fees) must be 'reasonably available' and that 'I can't say whether "slower" makes a bank transfer unreasonable', while treating the free transfer as the fee-free option, which matches 'may satisfy'. The hardest point is covered by 'The regulation that prescribes "rent payment..." only takes effect on and after 31 March 2026... So on 15 January 2026, the documents don't show s 51A catching an app's card fee yet.'

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer makes neither prohibited claim: it says s 51A's prescribed matter takes effect only "on and after 31 March 2026" so "on 15 January 2026, the documents don't show s 51A catching an app's card fee yet," and it states that "a rent payment method with no additional costs is reasonably available to you" is required.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 111, dated 25 Nov 2025' (rta-1997-v111-2025-11-25.pdf, 97-109aa111) and the Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021 as 'version 005, dated 25 Nov 2025' (rt-regs-2021-v005-2025-11-25.pdf, 21-3sra005), both in force on 15 January 2026, and it relies on no other version (it correctly treats the 31 March 2026 rent-payment prescription as not yet in effect).

question: This is happening now, on 15 October 2019. I signed a lease and picked up the keys, but before moving in I found damp, mould and rotting timber in the house. What are my options? Can I cancel, ask for repairs, or ask for lower rent?
answer:
**Document used:** *Residential Tenancies Act 1997*, Authorised Version No. 088, "rta-1997-v088-2019-07-02.pdf", incorporating amendments as at 2 July 2019. Its metadata shows it in force from 2 July 2019 to 3 December 2019, so it covers 15 October 2019 [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## What the law says

- **The landlord must keep the premises in good repair.** The landlord "must ensure that the rented premises are maintained in good repair" (s 68) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Handover condition.** On the agreed move-in day the premises must be vacant and in a "reasonably clean condition". A tenant isn't required to move in if they aren't, and doesn't pay rent from the agreed day until they actually move in (s 65) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf). This section is about vacancy and cleanliness. The retrieved text doesn't mention damp, mould or rot in it.
- **Ending the agreement before you take possession.** The agreement terminates if you have not entered into possession and you give the landlord a notice of termination on the ground that the premises are "not in good repair", "unfit for human habitation" or "for any other reason unavailable for occupation" (s 226) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Unfit for habitation.** A tenant can also give a notice of intention to vacate if the premises are unfit for human habitation or unsafe. The notice can take effect on the day it is given or later (s 238) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## Your three options

**1. Cancel**
- Section 226 is the most relevant provision, because you haven't moved in [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- You would give written notice of termination to the landlord. The ground would be that the premises are not in good repair or are unfit for habitation. Written notice is my suggestion; s 226 as retrieved doesn't say how the notice must be given.
- The documents don't say whether collecting the keys counts as "entering into possession". They don't define the term, so I can't say whether s 226 or s 238 is the safer route.
- I also can't tell you whether damp, mould and rotting timber amount to "unfit for human habitation". The retrieved text doesn't define that phrase.

**2. Ask for repairs**
- **Urgent repairs (s 72–73):**
  - You may arrange urgent repairs yourself if you have taken reasonable steps to get the landlord or agent to do them immediately and couldn't.
  - You must then give the landlord 14 days' written notice of the repairs and the cost. The landlord must reimburse the reasonable cost, or $1000, whichever is less.
  - If you can't meet the cost, the repairs cost more than $1000, or the landlord refuses to pay, you can apply to the Tribunal. It must hear the application within 2 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
  - The definition of "urgent repairs" wasn't in the retrieved text, so I can't confirm that mould, damp or rot qualifies.
- **Non-urgent repairs (s 74–76):**
  1. Give the landlord written notice that repairs are needed.
  2. If they aren't done within 14 days, apply in writing to the Director, who must investigate and give you a written report.
  3. Apply to the Tribunal within 60 days of receiving the report. You can also apply without a report if you haven't received one within 90 days of applying for it.
  4. The Tribunal can order specified repairs, with a deadline, if the landlord is in breach of the duty to maintain the premises in good repair [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Rent into the Rent Special Account (s 77):** after you have given notice requiring repairs, you can apply to the Tribunal to pay rent into this account. The Tribunal may order it if the landlord has failed to do the repairs [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- **Exception (s 80):** you can't use ss 72–75 where the breach results from a declaration under s 64 of the *Housing Act 1983* that the house is unfit for habitation [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

**3. Ask for lower rent**
- The retrieved text has no provision letting a tenant reduce rent on their own because of disrepair.
- The nearest provisions are the excessive-rent provisions. Under s 46, a tenant can apply to the Tribunal for an order declaring rent or proposed rent excessive, after a Director's report under s 45. A tenant who has received a rent increase notice can also apply, with the Tribunal's leave, under s 46(3). The Tribunal must declare the rent excessive if it is more than should reasonably be paid, having regard to factors that include "the state of repair and general condition of the rented premises" (s 47(3)(b)). It can direct a maximum rent for 12 months and order a refund (ss 47–48) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).
- The parts of s 45 that set out when a tenant can complain about the starting rent weren't retrieved. I can't confirm this route fits your situation.
- Section 65(3) only waives rent between the agreed move-in day and actual occupation. It applies where the premises weren't vacant and reasonably clean [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

## A caveat about the text

The same document also contains amending-Act text in its endnotes, using terms such as "renter" and "residential rental provider". Those passages include a new s 91L and a wider definition of urgent repairs that mentions mould and damp. The retrieved text doesn't show that these were in force on 15 October 2019, so I haven't relied on them. I've used the operative sections quoted above [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/b45d24ec-5984-3225-b9f1-f61b16fc197c_97-109aa088%20authorised.pdf).

I'd recommend getting advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria or a tenancy advocate before you send any notice. The documents don't answer whether collecting the keys means you have taken possession.

question: I am asking on Tuesday 8 November 2022. I signed a lease through an agency and paid the bond and the first month's rent. Now the agent says the owner will manage the place themselves and has sent me new bank details for the rent. What should I check before I pay into the new account?
answer:
# Rent paid to new bank details after a switch from agent to owner (Victoria, as at 8 November 2022)

**Sources used:** *rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Act 1997, version 101, in force 7 Sep 2022 to 23 May 2023, so it covers 8 Nov 2022) [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). I also used *rt-regs-2021-v002-2022-06-01.pdf* (Residential Tenancies Regulations 2021, version 002, in force from 1 Jun 2022) [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). The excerpts I retrieved don't print an "Authorised Version No." line. The version numbers above come from the documents' metadata.

## What the law says

- **Rent follows the agreement.** Rent is payable at the place and in the manner specified in the agreement [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The rental provider and renter can change the manner of payment *by agreement* [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The documents don't say whether a new bank account counts as a change of "manner", so check what your lease says.
- **Changes of agent or contact details need written notice.** If an agent is acting, the provider must give the renter the agent's name, address for service and phone/fax numbers. If there is no agent, the provider must give their own full name, address for service and an emergency phone number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). Any change in that information must be notified in writing within 7 days of the change. The penalty is 60 penalty units [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The standard lease form carries the same 7-day note [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf).
- **Payment options.** The provider or their agent must make a payment method with no extra cost (other than your own bank fees) reasonably available. They must also allow Centrepay and any prescribed method [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). They must tell you about any costs of a payment method before you consent to it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Receipts.** Whoever receives rent must give a written receipt immediately if you pay in person. If you don't pay in person, they must give one within 5 business days of a request made when you pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The receipt must be signed and state your name and the premises, the date, the period paid, the amount, and that it is for rent [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If no receipt is required, the recipient must keep a record for 12 months, and give you a copy within 5 business days of a request [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
- **Bond.** The provider must lodge your bond with the Authority within 10 business days [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). The Authority must send you a receipt within 7 days of getting it [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). If you haven't had a receipt within 15 business days of paying, you may notify the Authority [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What you can check or ask for

1. **Get the change in writing.** Ask for written notice from the owner of the change from agent to owner-managed. It should give the owner's full name, address for service and an emergency phone number [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf). A bank-details message alone doesn't meet this.
2. **Check your lease.** Look at the payment details and preferred methods in your agreement [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). Ask that any change to how or where you pay be agreed with you [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
3. **Confirm the owner's identity.** Compare the owner's name with the provider named in your lease and the bond lodgment form, and with your Authority bond receipt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf)[[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf). If ownership has actually been transferred, the provider must notify the Authority within 5 days and give you a copy of that notice [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
4. **Ask about costs.** Confirm the new account has no extra fees for you, and ask for fee information before you agree [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
5. **Ask for a receipt every time.** Request a signed receipt with the details listed above when you pay [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).
6. **Check your bond.** Confirm you received the Authority's bond receipt [[1]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-09/97-109aa101%20authorised.pdf).

## What the documents don't cover

- They don't say whether the agent's authority ends on a set date, or whether you can keep paying the agent until you receive proper written notice.
- They contain nothing on verifying bank details or avoiding payment scams. Phoning the agent on a number you already hold, and the owner separately, to confirm the account before paying is my own practical suggestion, not something in these documents.

For a dispute, the documents point to the Director of Consumer Affairs Victoria and VCAT [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf), but they don't say how either would handle a payment-details problem. I'd suggest getting advice from Consumer Affairs Victoria (1300 558 181, the number given in the lease form [[2]](https://content.legislation.vic.gov.au/sites/default/files/2022-06/21-3sra002%20authorised.pdf)).

must-mention.reason: Yes. All three points are covered. (1) The answer states that the provider must give their full name, address for service and an emergency phone number, and that any change must be notified in writing within 7 days. (2) It states that the bond must be lodged with the Authority within 10 business days, and it advises the renter to confirm they received the Authority's bond receipt. (3) It states that the provider and renter 'can change the manner of payment by agreement', and it recommends 'phoning the agent on a number you already hold, and the owner separately, to confirm the account before paying'.

must-not-say.reason: Yes. The answer never says the renter can stop paying rent; it only notes the documents don't say 'whether you can keep paying the agent until you receive proper written notice'. It also never says payment details can change without notice, stating instead that 'Any change in that information must be notified in writing within 7 days' and that the manner of payment can change only 'by agreement'.

version-cited.reason: Yes. The answer names the Residential Tenancies Act 1997 as 'version 101' (file rta-1997-v101-2022-09-07.pdf, link 97-109aa101), which is the version in force on 8 November 2022. The only other document it relies on is the Regulations 'version 002' (21-3sra002), also in force on that date, and it applies no rule from any other version.
